title: 'An £8k service charge left me unable to pay bills'
content_c:
'An £8k service charge left me unable to pay bills'
- Published
A housing association has defended the charges faced by its leaseholders after many complained of huge bill increases to pay for maintenance.
Callum Maddern, who lives in Bath, said he had seen his service charge increase six-fold to more than £8,000 per year after Curo said vital work needed doing on his accommodation block.
"I didn't have enough money to put the heating on," he said. "I had water on my sink and coffee tables that was freezing. I'd be lying in bed and I could see my breath."
Curo, which says it does not make any money from the contributions, said it was "trying to work with residents to prepare them for these bills".
More from Bristol
- Man jailed for 'cruel' attack that killed pensioner 
  - Published14 hours ago
- Community ownership could restore city landmark 
  - Published15 hours ago
- Student who murdered uni housemate jailed for life 
  - Published17 hours ago
When Callum bought his flat in 2023, the annual service charge was about £1,300 per year. He was told there was £5,000 in what is known as a sinking fund to cover any necessary works.
But the following year, he received a bill for £8,000 to go towards fire safety work and new windows.
"Originally I thought there was some kind of mistake," he said. But when he queried the charge, Curo confirmed it was accurate.
Callum describes "constant delays" in his attempts to reach out to Curo and negotiate.
"They were totally uncaring," he said, adding he was told he could sell his property and pay the fee that way.
Callum said he ended up selling possessions and taking out loans to pay for the work.
While he said he knew that as a leaseholder he had a responsibility to contribute towards maintenance costs, he questioned why everything suddenly had to be done in a three-year period.
"If new windows are needed, absolutely that must be scheduled in. But to have everything in the space of three years, surely that is not a good approach," Callum added.
'A perfect storm'
Andrew Snee, director of housing and support at Curo, acknowledged the way charges had been communicated could have been better and said he wanted to apologise "if our correspondence has caused any concern or upset".
But Snee denied the company could have managed the costs better, describing the situation as a "perfect storm".
"The cost of living is increasing, the cost of contracts is increasing, at the same time we've got increased legislation around property safety and fire safety, which has to be a good thing but it does come at a cost," he said.
"We are being as honest and transparent as we can to deliver these costs in as caring a way as we can. Keep talking to us."
Ken Pearson owns his flat in a different block elsewhere in Bath.
He says his sinking fund contributions dropped to £124 per year when Curo took over his building, but then increased dramatically to £1,767 when a new roof was needed.
"We were only being prepared for the new roof when it was a matter of urgency because two flats upstairs had leaks," he said. "We should have paid over a longer period."
Ken took Curo to a tribunal over the sinking fund increases and lost his case, but now believes there needs to be a change in the law to ensure that landlords prepare leaseholders better for expected works.
"Curo have failed us and need to be held to account," he said. "They have not picked up that there was this financial catastrophe coming along."
In response, Snee said: "I think sinking funds have been managed as well as we can in today's world with all of the pressures on costs and contracts."
He added: "If you've been building a sinking fund up and decoration has taken place, that would have potentially drawn quite a lot out.
"Then if you're looking at a roof replacement in four to five years' time, not only are you looking at paying for that you're also starting from zero."
The government is working on a new law that would ban the use of leasehold for most new flats and create a new right for leaseholders to request improvements.

title: Man fined after 700 frozen and taxidermied animals found on Victorian property
content_c:
The white-walled room packed with magpies, galahs and sulphur-crested cockatoos, foxes and possums is eerily quiet. As a video pans across shelves filled with these and many other species, there is no flapping or squawking or hissing; the animals are frozen and silent.
They are among the more than 700 native animals that were found illegally taxidermied and frozen that were seized from the property of a Victorian antiques store owner last year.
On Tuesday, 74-year-old Glenn Richard Rollo was fined $10,000 by a court after he pleaded guilty to 13 charges, including selling and possessing protected and threatened wildlife and failing to provide treatment to a sick animal.
The regulator searched his property as part of a broader crackdown on the illegal wildlife trade, executing search warrants for the man’s store and home in April last year. Restrictions on selling and possessing threatened and protected species apply to both living and dead animals.
During their search they found 14 freezers containing animals. Across the property they found hundreds of dead reptiles, native birds and mammals, including 78 emus, 42 brushtail possums and 26 echidnas. They also found the remains of threatened species, including the barking owl, diamond python and Murray River short-necked turtle.
In addition to the dead animals, 15 live reptiles were found in enclosures, including North American red-eared slider turtles and corn snakes. Six of the reptiles, the regulator said, were not being kept under the required animal welfare standards.
The regulator said the man did not have the licence of authorisation under Victoria’s wildlife laws to obtain or possess the animals.
Wildlife in Victoria is protected under the Wildlife Act 1975, which outlaws taking native animals without approval. A commercial wildlife licence or private wildlife licence is required to trade dead animals.
Victorians who wish to taxidermy animals are also required obtain a licence under the conservation regulator. The man did not hold a licence.
During an appearance before Kynton local court on Tuesday, magistrate Patrick Southey reportedly told the man: “It is bewildering that a man of your intelligence and knowledge and love of wildlife would arrogantly flout the law so comprehensively.”
The conservation regulator director of regulatory operations, Cal Heppell, said: “The scale of offending in this case highlights why Victoria has strong protections in place for wildlife and animal welfare.
“Our laws and permit systems help protect wildlife from unlawful exploitation, ensure animals are appropriately cared for and safeguard Victoria’s environment and biodiversity from potential threats.
“These requirements are not optional. Anyone who keeps, trades or possesses wildlife must comply with the law.”
Victoria Animal Justice party MP Georgie Purcell said the wildlife laws in Victoria are not strong enough and called on the government to modernise the 50-year-old welfare act.
 
 
 “This is a horrific case that has rattled our community of Kyneton but it should serve as a wake-up call as to just how broken our so-called wildlife protection laws are here in Victoria,” she said.
 
 
 Purcell said that the $10,000 fine for possessing 700 dead native animals and keeping reptiles in poor conditions was “barely a deterrent and doesn’t send a message to the community that wildlife are respected and protected in Victoria”.
 
 
 “The government talks a big game about protecting wildlife but cases like this show just how badly our native animals are being let down. If hundreds of native animals can end up dead in someone’s collection, questions need to be asked why the government has continued to stall when it comes to ensuring these laws meet community expectations.”

title: As Miatta ignites the speaker’s gas-fuelled inferno, Reform show up as snowflakes | John Crace
content_c:
When is a licence not a licence? When it’s a new licence that is an old licence. After months of faffing around – there were the small matters of a party conference and a byelection to negotiate first – the government finally gave the go-ahead to drilling in the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea. What swung it wasn’t so much the irresistible excitement of creating 27 new jobs and securing 2% of the UK’s gas supply for the next 10 years, it was the politics. If other countries were going to carry on drilling then we might as well do so, too.
There would still be the same amount of greenhouse gases created and we wouldn’t have to rely on anyone else for our gas supply. Though we would for the other 98%. Small steps and all that. At a time of global insecurity and rising energy costs, it was time to drill, baby, drill. So the inconvenience of a Labour manifesto that promised no new North Sea licences could be rethought. It was now merely re-allowing a licence that had already been granted and then deemed unlawful by the courts. AKA dancing on the head of the pin.
Donald Trump greeted the decision with wild enthusiasm. Though he appeared to be under the impression Jackdaw would be drilling for oil and would turn the UK into a land of plenty overnight. No one in the UK could quite bring themselves to enlighten him. Fair to say, that not everyone in the UK was quite so thrilled. Not least Ed Miliband, the former energy secretary, and Miatta Fahnbulleh, the current one.
Miatta had sought permission to be as far away as possible from Westminster for prime minister’s questions and the subsequent ministerial statement on Jackdaw. So she had taken the trouble to go all the way to Aberdeen to make a television statement that she could have made in her own department. And she is the one worried about her carbon footprint.
Only it turns out that any amount of emissions is a price worth paying for a minister anxious not to have the hypocrisy of her former opposition to Jackdaw replayed to her by many of her own backbench MPs. Life comes at you fast when you’re a politician climbing the greasy ministerial pole. You find yourself in some awkward places, the most awkward being the House of Commons. Hence the – ahem – unfortunate diary clash.
The speaker was less than impressed. Lindsay Hoyle sounded as if he had swallowed a fistful of amphetamines and steroids and was mid-roid rage. He only just stopped short of calling the Labour frontbench a bunch of fucking fucks. Maybe he was just having a bad day.
For decades now, governments of all colours have been going out of their way to make sure that junior ministers take the flak to save their bosses the embarrassment of an hour’s humiliation at the dispatch box. The parliamentary equivalent of droit de seigneur. Lindsay demanded assurances this would never happen again, and the junior energy minister Michael Shanks duly nodded sheepishly. Not that he cared. He mainlines oil for breakfast. Inside, he was just counting down the seconds till the speaker had calmed down a bit. And then carried on as normal. Of course it will happen again. Maybe even next week.
PMQs itself also took on a familiar look, with Kemi Badenoch unable to make any inroads into Andy Burnham. You could even sense her frustration. There were times when she could get under Keir Starmer’s skin, but now both she and the Labour party have seen him off, she is faced with Mr Congeniality.
Against him, Kemi’s attack lines feel half-arsed. Not properly thought through. Everything she tries just bounces off him. He seems almost untouchable. Mostly because he’s a better politician, but also because he has the air of a reasonable grownup. Someone you feel is doing his best and comes across as someone you can trust. Well. As close to honest as you get in Westminster.
By contrast, Kemi feels like a second-rate opportunist. She tried making something of Labour taking years to approve the Jackdaw licence, a charge that rather melted away when Burnham pointed out we could have been drilling ages ago if the Tories had bothered to get the necessary legalities right in the first place. This was about putting pragmatism before ideology, Andy insisted. Fair enough. Though expect him to say precisely the opposite when it comes to the Rosebank oilfield. Then ideology will take precedence over pragmatism. Fahnbulleh had already as good as confirmed that Rosebank was dead in the water.
For the rest of PMQs, it was Kemi who was dead in the water. Seemingly having no other real questions she wanted to ask. It felt like she was sulking. Or underprepared. Her pre-budget attack lines went nowhere. First Andy pointed out that he was the only one with a plan to ditch the triple lock and sort out social care – still more vibes than policy – and ended by making fun of Liz Truss’s forthcoming new book on the mini-budget.
It wasn’t her who had screwed the country, apparently. Liz had been captured by the Blob. But it could have been any number of the current members of the shadow cabinet. Including the shadow chancellor who was part of the Trusster’s team. Incidentally, Liz was due to be interviewed by a robot on Wednesday afternoon at a Lincolnshire fair. But how would we know which was which?
That just left time for Burnham to take one question from a Labour backbencher about the ITV exposé of Reform. Though Nigel Farage had already left the chamber by then, so he couldn’t get all heated and declare that it was all a London plot and that it was perfectly normal for people to be as racist as possible in the comfort of their own homes. It was political correctness gone mad.
As if by telepathy, Zia Yusuf had chosen just that moment to post a video on social media in which he expressed his immense sadness that the media had stooped so low. He would be reporting ITV to the police, he insisted, because they had betrayed the racist code of honour.
How could everyday racists feel comfortable expressing their racism in the workplace if they couldn’t be sure that their colleagues weren’t undercover journalists looking to expose them? The world had gone mad. Who would have guessed that deep down, Zia – the man even the Reform elite have come to hate – was a snowflake at heart.

What swung it wasn’t so much the irresistible excitement of creating 27 new jobs and securing 2% of the UK’s gas supply for the next 10 years, it was the politics. If other countries were going to carry on drilling then we might as well do so, too.
There would still be the same amount of greenhouse gases created and we wouldn’t have to rely on anyone else for our gas supply. Though we would for the other 98%. Small steps and all that. At a time of global insecurity and rising energy costs, it was time to drill, baby, drill. So the inconvenience of a Labour manifesto that promised no new North Sea licences could be rethought. It was now merely re-allowing a licence that had already been granted and then deemed unlawful by the courts. AKA dancing on the head of the pin.
Donald Trump greeted the decision with wild enthusiasm. Though he appeared to be under the impression Jackdaw would be drilling for oil and would turn the UK into a land of plenty overnight. No one in the UK could quite bring themselves to enlighten him. Fair to say, that not everyone in the UK was quite so thrilled. Not least Ed Miliband, the former energy secretary, and Miatta Fahnbulleh, the current one.
Miatta had sought permission to be as far away as possible from Westminster for prime minister’s questions and the subsequent ministerial statement on Jackdaw. So she had taken the trouble to go all the way to Aberdeen to make a television statement that she could have made in her own department. And she is the one worried about her carbon footprint.
Only it turns out that any amount of emissions is a price worth paying for a minister anxious not to have the hypocrisy of her former opposition to Jackdaw replayed to her by many of her own backbench MPs. Life comes at you fast when you’re a politician climbing the greasy ministerial pole. You find yourself in some awkward places, the most awkward being the House of Commons. Hence the – ahem – unfortunate diary clash.
The speaker was less than impressed. Lindsay Hoyle sounded as if he had swallowed a fistful of amphetamines and steroids and was mid-roid rage. He only just stopped short of calling the Labour frontbench a bunch of fucking fucks. Maybe he was just having a bad day.
For decades now, governments of all colours have been going out of their way to make sure that junior ministers take the flak to save their bosses the embarrassment of an hour’s humiliation at the dispatch box. The parliamentary equivalent of droit de seigneur. Lindsay demanded assurances this would never happen again, and the junior energy minister Michael Shanks duly nodded sheepishly. Not that he cared. He mainlines oil for breakfast. Inside, he was just counting down the seconds till the speaker had calmed down a bit. And then carried on as normal. Of course it will happen again. Maybe even next week.
PMQs itself also took on a familiar look, with Kemi Badenoch unable to make any inroads into Andy Burnham. You could even sense her frustration. There were times when she could get under Keir Starmer’s skin, but now both she and the Labour party have seen him off, she is faced with Mr Congeniality.
Against him, Kemi’s attack lines feel half-arsed. Not properly thought through. Everything she tries just bounces off him. He seems almost untouchable. Mostly because he’s a better politician, but also because he has the air of a reasonable grownup. Someone you feel is doing his best and comes across as someone you can trust. Well. As close to honest as you get in Westminster.
By contrast, Kemi feels like a second-rate opportunist. She tried making something of Labour taking years to approve the Jackdaw licence, a charge that rather melted away when Burnham pointed out we could have been drilling ages ago if the Tories had bothered to get the necessary legalities right in the first place. This was about putting pragmatism before ideology, Andy insisted. Fair enough. Though expect him to say precisely the opposite when it comes to the Rosebank oilfield. Then ideology will take precedence over pragmatism. Fahnbulleh had already as good as confirmed that Rosebank was dead in the water.
For the rest of PMQs, it was Kemi who was dead in the water. Seemingly having no other real questions she wanted to ask. It felt like she was sulking. Or underprepared. Her pre-budget attack lines went nowhere. First Andy pointed out that he was the only one with a plan to ditch the triple lock and sort out social care – still more vibes than policy – and ended by making fun of Liz Truss’s forthcoming new book on the mini-budget.
It wasn’t her who had screwed the country, apparently. Liz had been captured by the Blob. But it could have been any number of the current members of the shadow cabinet. Including the shadow chancellor who was part of the Trusster’s team. Incidentally, Liz was due to be interviewed by a robot on Wednesday afternoon at a Lincolnshire fair. But how would we know which was which?
That just left time for Burnham to take one question from a Labour backbencher about the ITV exposé of Reform. Though Nigel Farage had already left the chamber by then, so he couldn’t get all heated and declare that it was all a London plot and that it was perfectly normal for people to be as racist as possible in the comfort of their own homes. It was political correctness gone mad.
As if by telepathy, Zia Yusuf had chosen just that moment to post a video on social media in which he expressed his immense sadness that the media had stooped so low. He would be reporting ITV to the police, he insisted, because they had betrayed the racist code of honour.
How could everyday racists feel comfortable expressing their racism in the workplace if they couldn’t be sure that their colleagues weren’t undercover journalists looking to expose them? The world had gone mad. Who would have guessed that deep down, Zia – the man even the Reform elite have come to hate – was a snowflake at heart.

Germany news: AfD's Weidel calls for major EU reforms
Published October 21, 2026last updated October 22, 2026
What you need to know
- 
	One of Weidel's reforms is for European parliamentarians to no longer be directly elected
- 
	Nvidia's Jensen Huang had words of encouragement for Europe's growing AI economy during a conference in Berlin
- 
	Germany's Finance Ministry has erroneously introduced an approved tax hike on tobacco products months before it was scheduled to come into effect
- 
	Germany's Bundesbank has forecast growth for the fourth quarter after a dip in the third quarter
This blog is now closed. Below is a round-up of top stories from and about Germany on Wednesday, October 21, 2026.
Thanks for following our blog
We'll be back with the latest headlines out of the country on Thursday. Tschüss!
Weidel pitches 'three pillars' of EU reform at European Parliament
Alice Weidel, the co-leader of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, has presented her party's proposals for a European Union that she said was "in severe need of reform" during a visit to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, saying they rested on three core pillars.
"We would like to rebuild and reform the European Union," she said. "We would like to found the European Union on three major principles: the first one is subsidiarity, the second one is responsibility, and the third one is sovereignty."
On subsidiarity — the idea that power should reside as close to the grassroots level as possible as much as possible — she said it was important to put the "competences" on the "lowest level of decision-making," saying "we don't want the state, or the [European] Commission — that is not elected — to intrude and disturb your private life in decision-making."
"I'm an economist, and for me, the European Union is not a group of sovereign states any more," Weidel said. She said that in sovereign states' parliaments, leaders were elected, "and so the decision-making on the sovereign level should be made in the national parliaments and not here, to be very clear."
This is already the case in the vast majority of core EU public policy areas. National governments decide foreign and defense issues, finance and health policy, education policy and much more. The notable exceptions Weidel objects to are fiscal policy and the primacy of EU law, but only after sovereign member states agree to them.
She said the European Commission was not elected but had a "legislative right of initiative," saying this was a "huge disturbance of checks and balances" and of a "democratic decision-making process."
Weidel accused the EU of failing to follow its own rules, for instance on sovereign debt and whether the European Central Bank should or can guarantee it, citing issues like this as questions of responsibility.
Finally, she reiterated her desire for "sovereign states to protect their borders," saying that "if the European Union is not capable of protecting our borders, the outer borders ... then it is a decision of the sovereign states to protect our national borders."
"If Schengen is over, if Schengen doesn't work, then we need to get out of Schengen and protect our borders," she said of the open-border zone within much of the EU.
She said that if the EU fails to protect the bloc's external borders, "we should have a veto right to opt out of this chaos."
While the EU maintains a border management agency, Frontex, national authorities are responsible for the external borders of the Schengen zone and the EU.
WATCH — Journalist says Merz 'sounds very much like Trump'
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz criticized China for "unfair practices" in trade, and said he wants EU member states to balance out their trade deficits.
That elicited a bold comparison from a journalist who said, "You sound very much like Donald Trump."
Watch the exchange here:
Nvidia CEO Huang dazzles Berlin audience with AI pitch
A massive stage, all in black. A colorful laser light show. Upbeat music. AI-generated videos on a gigantic screen. On stage, just one man in a black leather jacket: Jensen Huang, the 63-year-old CEO of Nvidia, which manufactures superfast computer chips needed for AI data centers and happens to be the world's most valuable company.
The relaxed Nvidia boss set out his vision of the upcoming AI revolution and, of course, the products Nvidia has developed for the "second wave" of AI. The 4,000 attendees at Berlin's Tempodrom arena were thrilled by what Jensen Huang had to say (see entry below).
Huang said Germany and Europe could be part of the next industrial revolution — not as developers of AI language models or computer chips, but as producers of robots, machines, tools, and entire factories controlled by AI applications.
"You have to transfer AI into the real world of production," he said. Europe could use its data to train AI and develop customized models for automakers, pharmaceutical companies, and many small and medium-sized businesses.
Unsurprisingly, Nvidia offers all the AI software and hardware needed to get in on the action. A new addition to the Nvidia universe is a "Giga-Factory," which is housed in modular shipping containers and can be set up in just a few days or weeks anywhere with a suitable power grid.
There was also something for consumers: a high-performance laptop with a built-in AI agent that acts as a "friend and helper," capable of taking over tasks and programming new agents. Huang went on to demonstrate four small robot ducks that had been trained by this AI agent to perform cute tricks, which were met with laughter and applause.
But it wasn't all cheers. A woman in the audience interrupted a product demo to point out that AI is also used to control Russian drones. She was escorted out by security guards, but Huang assured the audience that he would speak with her later. He was keen to add that Nvidia has also developed a security system designed to keep AI agents in check and prevent misuse.
Nvidia is now valued at €5 trillion ($5.6 trillion) on the stock market. That is roughly equivalent to the total economic output of all of Germany in 2025.
German Bundeswehr sees 'significant' threat of sabotage
The German military, known as the Bundeswehr, has rated the threat of sabotage against it as "significant," according to a reports by the Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) and public broadcaster WDR.
A spokesperson for the Defense Ministry pointed to several recent cases, including the discovery of a drone close to an airbase in Wunstorf and acts of sabotage against Navy ships.
The military is looking to increase security to counter the threat, with the ministry spokesperson naming increased surveillance at airports and military docks by soldiers or infrared cameras.
"The incidents highlight the ability that Russia has almost certainly had for a while now, as well as very likely the increased intention, to act against Bundeswehr forces and facilities, as well as partners such as Ukraine in Germany," SZ reported based on internal military analysis.
The aim is therefore "very likely an intention to degrade the current political and society-wide German support for Ukraine."
The ministry spokesperson also pointed out that the incidents did not mark a major change, with the military facing similar challenges over the past decades.
He said "automatic defense concepts" are in place for acute terror threats, but "we are not at that point."
German imports from Russia plunge, but not to zero
German trade with Russia collapsed following the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, especially due to the decision to cut all imports of Russian gas. However, some trade has continued.
According to the German Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), German imports of Russian goods were down by 96.4% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period in 2021.
This amounted to €500 million ($561 million) in 2026, down from €15 billion. German exports to Russia were also down, but still significant, reaching €3.4 billion in the first six months of 2026. However, this was about a quarter of the exports in the same period in 2021.
Pharmaceutical products made up more than 40% of German exports to Russia, with machinery, food and animal feed also being exported in smaller quantities.
Nvidia CEO urges Europe to build more data centers
Jensen Huang, the head of chip manufacturing giant Nvidia, was speaking at a company conference for developers and investors in Berlin's Tempodrom auditorium on Wednesday.
He was seeking to encourage Europe to build out its data center infrastructure and touted Nvidia's modular tools to help speed up that process.
"Europe's AI economy is starting, and it's accelerating, and it's great to see," Huang said.
He promoted a new design for a ready-made modular computing center that comes in a box akin to a shipping container and that could make it possible to construct a data center in a matter of days. Huang said it "will change the way people build AI centers."
Nvidia has invested $10 billion (€8.9 billion) in European startups over the past year, the Nvidia boss said.
Europe has fallen behind the US and China in terms of building up data centers and is currently home to around 5% of the world's AI computing capacity in comparison to 75% in the US. This capacity is required to train AI models and its lack is seen as a major obstacle for European developers.
Most current data centers are reliant on Nvidia GPUs to run.
Financial Ministry admits mistake, says tobacco tax coming January 1 as planned
A spokesperson for Germany's Federal Financial Ministry on Wednesday addressed confusion surrounding the implementation of a new tobacco tax saying, "The tax increase in the law's wording was approved to go into effect on January 1, 2027, that remains the case."
The spokesperson confirmed that the mix-up over when the new law would take effect resulted from a technical error that put the law on the books immediately rather than January 1 as intended.
The issue stemmed from a mistake in the government's original writing of the law.
Customs officials have reportedly been informed and the Financial Ministry's website makes clear that the price increase will not be charged until the beginning of the new year.
German youth plans France-style mass protests
"Gen Z regelt" — or Gen Z's Got It — a youth initiative, has called for mass protests in 21 cities across Germany on Saturday, October 31; including Berlin, Cologne, Hamburg and Munich.
Thousands are expected to participate in demonstrations protesting "broken schools and austerity," as well as the cost of living, social injustice, military conscription and climate change.
French protests that exploded in violence and rampant destruction of private and public property this weekend also grew out of student frustration over the national school system and soon included numerous unions, groups and individuals voicing anger over a number of issues.
Gen Z regelt's website clearly states that the initiative is "against all violence," whether directed at people or property.
Police say they are "vigilant and relaxed," adding that they intend to protect people's right to congregate and express their opinions.
Still, images of massive damage and public violence from France, Italy and Spain have raised concerns among domestic policymakers and police, who have warned against allowing the protests to be hijacked by left-wing extremists.
Andreas Roßkopf, head of the German Federal Police's GdP union, made clear that officers would deal harshly with riots and rioters, telling the Rheinische Post newspaper on Wednesday, "State, but also federal police, will offer a firm and decisive response" to any trouble.
Roßkopf also warned that radicals and extremists could insert themselves among demonstrators in order to "attack police" or "simply be destructive."
Bundesbank forecasts German growth for Q4
The Bundesbank, Germany's central bank, has said it is expecting to see an uptick in growth for Europe's biggest economy in the fourth quarter.
"German economic output is likely to improve again markedly in the fourth quarter," the bank said in its monthly report on Wednesday. "However, the future economic recovery depends, not least, on the development of the war in the Middle East."
The optimistic outlook follows a dip in the third quarter, which the bank chalked up largely to this summer's drought that caused such low water levels in the Rhine River, an artery in western Germany for industry, that most ships could not travel.
"The low water levels are also likely to continue to have a negative impact on foreign trade via European ports as a result of restrictions on inland water transport," the bank wrote.
The forecast will be welcomed by the Merz government as it has struggled to boost the economy after two consecutive years of recession followed by weak growth in 2025.
Merz: EU doesn't want trade war with China
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said he does not think Europe is on course for a trade war with China while acknowledging what he called "unfair practice" on the part of Beijing.
Speaking at a business conference in Berlin, Merz said the imbalance did not mean "the beginning of a war, of a trade war with China. We are looking for peaceful solutions, but the level for that is fair trade."
The German chancellor has been pushing for the EU to be better prepared for trade disputes with China, including calling for a means to quickly exclude non-EU countries from the EU's single market if they flood it with cheap goods.
Merz said the EU needs to be able "to protect our markets and defend ourselves against those who don't play by the rules."
"Anyone who disrupts the functioning of the markets through unfair subsidies, overcapacities, aggressive pricing, or artificially undervalued currencies must expect a response," he said.
That includes tools that "enable us to respond swiftly and vigorously to targeted attacks on our industry and supply chain, with the idea being that in the best case we will not have to use it."
Ifo Institute questions savings target of parental allowance reform
Germany has a rather generous parental allowance system in comparison to many countries, with parents being able to take off 14 months, if each parent takes at least two months off, with the government paying up to €1,800 (just over $2,000) a month during that period.
However, this system has become the subject of a planned reform under the government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
The plan is to reduce the maximum amount of full-time paid parental leave to 12 months. With three months each reserved for both parents and the remaining six months free to be divided up however the parents choose. It also raises the minimum payment from €300 to €330 and the maximum from €1,800 to €1,900.
The government's aim is to make cuts to help the Ministry for Family Affairs reach its savings target of €1.6 billion, while also encouraging more fathers to take parental leave. Currently, fewer than half of fathers in Germany take parental leave.
Now the Ifo Institute for Economic Research has cast doubts on the government's savings plan.
"The savings target and the goal of increasing fathers’ participation in the planned parental allowance reform are at odds with each other. The higher the number of fathers who are motivated to participate by the reform, the less the government saves," Ifo researcher Kyra Puteanus said.
The institute estimates savings of around €880 million from November 2027, when the reform comes into effect. However, if more fathers, who generally earn more and thus are able to request the highest payment, do take up the parental leave, this will quickly reduce the savings, with Ifo predicting that even if the uptake by fathers only increases by 1%, savings will fall to €597 million. An increase of 3.1% would undo any savings from the reform, according to the institute.
"Since 2010, however, the share of fathers receiving parental allowance has almost doubled. A rapid increase can therefore not be ruled out, especially if months are otherwise forfeited," Ifo researcher Franziska Nuernbergk said.
IDF says it killed Hamas member involved in abduction of German dual national
The Israel Defense Forces (IFD) said in a post on X that they have killed Tamer Mohammad Ibrahim Al-Zabaq, a member of the Hamas terror group who was involved in the October 7 attacks.
The post said that al-Zabaq had been one of the men responsible for the abduction of Shani Louk, a dual German-Israeli national.
Louk was initially thought to have been taken hostage following the Hamas-led attacks but it was later confirmed that she had been killed.
In the immediate aftermath of the terror attacks, pictures and videos shared online showed a young woman, believed to be Shani, lying face down in a pick-up truck driven by militants. It was unclear from the footage whether she was alive.
The IDF also accused Al-Zabaq of operating to "restore Hamas' military capabilities, in systematic violation of the ceasefire."
"The terrorist was eliminated in order to remove the threat he posed," the IDF said.
The claims in the X post could not be independently verified.
Israel has carried out numerous deadly strikes on Gaza since the ceasefire came into effect just over a year ago.
Merz calls on Trump to make sure South Africa is at G20
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, addressing the Business Global Dialogue summit in Berlin on Wednesday, renewed calls for US President Donald Trump to invite South Africa (a G20 member) to the upcoming G20 summit that he will host in Miami this December.
"Whoever talks about the future of the global economy must include all important partners. Of course Africa belongs at the table," he said, adding: "The African Union is a G20 member, as is South Africa. That is why I urgently insist that South Africa be represented at the G20 summit."
Merz made a similar plea last year, when Trump angrily insisted that he would not invite South Africa to the annual summit of the 20 leading industrial and emerging economies.
Trump has accused South Africa of committing genocide on white farmers and dismissed South African pushback against his repeated claim. The anti-immigrant president also took the unusual step of offering South Africans political asylum in the US — as long as they are white.
The US President is apparently less bothered by wars of aggression, extending an invitation to President Vladimir Putin to come to Miami, despite Russia being thrown out of the G8 — now G7 — over its 2014 invasion and annexation of Ukraine's Crimea.
Beyond his plea for South Africa's inclusion, Merz said he would travel to the US with what he called a "Miami Growth Agenda" aimed at slashing bureaucracy, pushing structural reforms and making investment easier.
"Those" he said, "are the prerequisites for new economic growth and prosperity, not only in Germany, but globally."
Russia arrests German national, says he's a 'mercenary' — reports
Russian FSB agents have arrested a German national, accusing him of being a mercenary under contract with the Ukrainian army.
"The Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation has detained a German citizen who is a serving member of the Armed Forces of Ukraine," said a statement cited by Russian news agencies.
The FSB says the man, whom they described as a sniper, previously fought in Afghanistan and Syria as well as in Ukraine between 2016 and 2018.
They say he arrived in Ukraine last November and signed a three-year contract with the Ukrainian army before deserting over unpaid wages.
Last week, the FSB arrested a Swedish national whom Russian authorities also accused of fighting on Kyiv's behalf.
Russia has arrested hundreds of foreign nationals that it accuses of "espionage," "sabotage" or "treason" to long prison sentences since it began its invasion of neighboring Ukraine.
A number of foreign nationals have also been jailed over supposed "mercenary activity."

Customs officials have reportedly been informed and the Financial Ministry's website makes clear that the price increase will not be charged until the beginning of the new year.
German youth plans France-style mass protests
"Gen Z regelt" — or Gen Z's Got It — a youth initiative, has called for mass protests in 21 cities across Germany on Saturday, October 31; including Berlin, Cologne, Hamburg and Munich.
Thousands are expected to participate in demonstrations protesting "broken schools and austerity," as well as the cost of living, social injustice, military conscription and climate change.
French protests that exploded in violence and rampant destruction of private and public property this weekend also grew out of student frustration over the national school system and soon included numerous unions, groups and individuals voicing anger over a number of issues.
Gen Z regelt's website clearly states that the initiative is "against all violence," whether directed at people or property.
Police say they are "vigilant and relaxed," adding that they intend to protect people's right to congregate and express their opinions.
Still, images of massive damage and public violence from France, Italy and Spain have raised concerns among domestic policymakers and police, who have warned against allowing the protests to be hijacked by left-wing extremists.
Andreas Roßkopf, head of the German Federal Police's GdP union, made clear that officers would deal harshly with riots and rioters, telling the Rheinische Post newspaper on Wednesday, "State, but also federal police, will offer a firm and decisive response" to any trouble.
Roßkopf also warned that radicals and extremists could insert themselves among demonstrators in order to "attack police" or "simply be destructive."
Bundesbank forecasts German growth for Q4
The Bundesbank, Germany's central bank, has said it is expecting to see an uptick in growth for Europe's biggest economy in the fourth quarter.
"German economic output is likely to improve again markedly in the fourth quarter," the bank said in its monthly report on Wednesday. "However, the future economic recovery depends, not least, on the development of the war in the Middle East."
The optimistic outlook follows a dip in the third quarter, which the bank chalked up largely to this summer's drought that caused such low water levels in the Rhine River, an artery in western Germany for industry, that most ships could not travel.
"The low water levels are also likely to continue to have a negative impact on foreign trade via European ports as a result of restrictions on inland water transport," the bank wrote.
The forecast will be welcomed by the Merz government as it has struggled to boost the economy after two consecutive years of recession followed by weak growth in 2025.
Merz: EU doesn't want trade war with China
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said he does not think Europe is on course for a trade war with China while acknowledging what he called "unfair practice" on the part of Beijing.
Speaking at a business conference in Berlin, Merz said the imbalance did not mean "the beginning of a war, of a trade war with China. We are looking for peaceful solutions, but the level for that is fair trade."
The German chancellor has been pushing for the EU to be better prepared for trade disputes with China, including calling for a means to quickly exclude non-EU countries from the EU's single market if they flood it with cheap goods.
Merz said the EU needs to be able "to protect our markets and defend ourselves against those who don't play by the rules."
"Anyone who disrupts the functioning of the markets through unfair subsidies, overcapacities, aggressive pricing, or artificially undervalued currencies must expect a response," he said.
That includes tools that "enable us to respond swiftly and vigorously to targeted attacks on our industry and supply chain, with the idea being that in the best case we will not have to use it."
Ifo Institute questions savings target of parental allowance reform
Germany has a rather generous parental allowance system in comparison to many countries, with parents being able to take off 14 months, if each parent takes at least two months off, with the government paying up to €1,800 (just over $2,000) a month during that period.
However, this system has become the subject of a planned reform under the government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
The plan is to reduce the maximum amount of full-time paid parental leave to 12 months. With three months each reserved for both parents and the remaining six months free to be divided up however the parents choose. It also raises the minimum payment from €300 to €330 and the maximum from €1,800 to €1,900.
The government's aim is to make cuts to help the Ministry for Family Affairs reach its savings target of €1.6 billion, while also encouraging more fathers to take parental leave. Currently, fewer than half of fathers in Germany take parental leave.
Now the Ifo Institute for Economic Research has cast doubts on the government's savings plan.
"The savings target and the goal of increasing fathers’ participation in the planned parental allowance reform are at odds with each other. The higher the number of fathers who are motivated to participate by the reform, the less the government saves," Ifo researcher Kyra Puteanus said.
The institute estimates savings of around €880 million from November 2027, when the reform comes into effect. However, if more fathers, who generally earn more and thus are able to request the highest payment, do take up the parental leave, this will quickly reduce the savings, with Ifo predicting that even if the uptake by fathers only increases by 1%, savings will fall to €597 million. An increase of 3.1% would undo any savings from the reform, according to the institute.
"Since 2010, however, the share of fathers receiving parental allowance has almost doubled. A rapid increase can therefore not be ruled out, especially if months are otherwise forfeited," Ifo researcher Franziska Nuernbergk said.
IDF says it killed Hamas member involved in abduction of German dual national
The Israel Defense Forces (IFD) said in a post on X that they have killed Tamer Mohammad Ibrahim Al-Zabaq, a member of the Hamas terror group who was involved in the October 7 attacks.
The post said that al-Zabaq had been one of the men responsible for the abduction of Shani Louk, a dual German-Israeli national.
Louk was initially thought to have been taken hostage following the Hamas-led attacks but it was later confirmed that she had been killed.
In the immediate aftermath of the terror attacks, pictures and videos shared online showed a young woman, believed to be Shani, lying face down in a pick-up truck driven by militants. It was unclear from the footage whether she was alive.
The IDF also accused Al-Zabaq of operating to "restore Hamas' military capabilities, in systematic violation of the ceasefire."
"The terrorist was eliminated in order to remove the threat he posed," the IDF said.
The claims in the X post could not be independently verified.
Israel has carried out numerous deadly strikes on Gaza since the ceasefire came into effect just over a year ago.
Merz calls on Trump to make sure South Africa is at G20
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, addressing the Business Global Dialogue summit in Berlin on Wednesday, renewed calls for US President Donald Trump to invite South Africa (a G20 member) to the upcoming G20 summit that he will host in Miami this December.
"Whoever talks about the future of the global economy must include all important partners. Of course Africa belongs at the table," he said, adding: "The African Union is a G20 member, as is South Africa. That is why I urgently insist that South Africa be represented at the G20 summit."
Merz made a similar plea last year, when Trump angrily insisted that he would not invite South Africa to the annual summit of the 20 leading industrial and emerging economies.
Trump has accused South Africa of committing genocide on white farmers and dismissed South African pushback against his repeated claim. The anti-immigrant president also took the unusual step of offering South Africans political asylum in the US — as long as they are white.
The US President is apparently less bothered by wars of aggression, extending an invitation to President Vladimir Putin to come to Miami, despite Russia being thrown out of the G8 — now G7 — over its 2014 invasion and annexation of Ukraine's Crimea.
Beyond his plea for South Africa's inclusion, Merz said he would travel to the US with what he called a "Miami Growth Agenda" aimed at slashing bureaucracy, pushing structural reforms and making investment easier.
"Those" he said, "are the prerequisites for new economic growth and prosperity, not only in Germany, but globally."
Russia arrests German national, says he's a 'mercenary' — reports
Russian FSB agents have arrested a German national, accusing him of being a mercenary under contract with the Ukrainian army.
"The Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation has detained a German citizen who is a serving member of the Armed Forces of Ukraine," said a statement cited by Russian news agencies.
The FSB says the man, whom they described as a sniper, previously fought in Afghanistan and Syria as well as in Ukraine between 2016 and 2018.
They say he arrived in Ukraine last November and signed a three-year contract with the Ukrainian army before deserting over unpaid wages.
Last week, the FSB arrested a Swedish national whom Russian authorities also accused of fighting on Kyiv's behalf.
Russia has arrested hundreds of foreign nationals that it accuses of "espionage," "sabotage" or "treason" to long prison sentences since it began its invasion of neighboring Ukraine.
A number of foreign nationals have also been jailed over supposed "mercenary activity."

title: News: Sicherheitsrisiko PHP, Kanzler im Westbalkan, Ministerpräsidentenkonferenz, Hubertus Heil
content_c:
Die Lage am Morgen Gespenstische Stille im Netz
- Die Programmiersprache PHP weist Sicherheitslücken auf – wie bedrohlich ist das?
- Der Kanzler reist in die Westbalkanregion – nimmt die EU dort neue Mitglieder auf?
- Die Ministerpräsidenten kommen zusammen – bald mit Beteiligung der AfD?
Im Offlinemodus
In vielen Ecken des Internets herrscht gespenstische Stille. Etliche Websites sind zeitweise nicht erreichbar, weil in der Programmiersprache PHP eine gravierende Sicherheitslücke aufgetreten ist.
Internetseite der Stadt Mainz am Mittwoch: Nicht erreichbar
Foto: Bernd Weißbrod / dpa
Zahlreiche Städte, Behörden, öffentliche Einrichtungen und private Firmen nehmen nun ihre Seiten zwischenzeitlich vom Netz. Als Vorsichtsmaßnahme, um drohenden Angriffen zuvorzukommen. Immerhin: Seit Mittwochnachmittag gibt es ein Update, mit dem sich die fehlerhaften Systeme absichern lassen.
Das Problem: Angreifer könnten schneller sein und Schadsoftware in die Webserver schmuggeln, bevor sie aktualisiert werden. Das Ausmaß ist noch nicht abzusehen, es könnte gewaltig sein. Schätzungen zufolge werden weltweit rund 70 Prozent aller Websites und Webanwendungen mit der Programmiersprache PHP betrieben. Von der Sicherheitslücke betroffen sind alle PHP-Versionen der vergangenen 20 Jahre. Bedroht wären somit etliche Millionen Seiten.
Die bange Frage lautet, wer schneller ist: Betreiber von Websites, die jetzt ihre Server absichern müssen, oder Angreifer, die sich die Lücke zunutze machen, um Daten abzugreifen und Seiten zu kapern?
- Mehr Hintergründe hier: Gleich zwei große Sicherheitslücken alarmieren Experten
Kurz mal an die Adria
Während einige seiner Koalitionskolleginnen und -kollegen im Urlaub weilen und das Kabinett deshalb in dieser Woche nicht zusammenkam, nutzt der Kanzler die innenpolitisch eher ruhige Zeit für Auslandsreisen. Heute ist Friedrich Merz in Montenegro. An der Adria berät der Kanzler mit Amtskollegen aus der Region und EU-Partnern über die Fortschritte beim Beitritt der Westbalkanstaaten zur EU. Wobei »Fortschritte« nicht ganz richtig ist. »Stillstand« trifft es besser.
Kanzler Merz in Berlin: Antreiber im Westbalkan
Foto: Clemens Bilan / EPA
Die Erweiterungspolitik der EU für die Länder des Westbalkans trägt Züge einer unendlichen Geschichte. Seit rund zwei Jahrzehnten hängen Montenegro, Serbien, Albanien, Nordmazedonien, Bosnien-Herzegowina und Kosovo in der Warteschleife fest. Ihre Regierungen sagen Reformen zu, die sie mal mehr, mal weniger beherzt angehen, was dann die EU-Kommission in ihren Berichten penibel dokumentiert. In der Sache passiert wenig. Seit dem Beitritt Kroatiens hat es kein weiterer Staat in die EU geschafft, und der liegt schon 13 Jahre zurück.
Merz treibt die Sorge um, dass sich die Länder des Westbalkans von der EU hingehalten fühlen und sich lieber anderen Mächten zuwenden, etwa Russland oder China. Deshalb schlug der Kanzler im vergangenen Sommer mit Frankreichs Präsident Emmanuel Macron vor, diese Staaten schon vor einer formellen EU-Mitgliedschaft enger an die EU zu binden. Etwa mit der Möglichkeit zur stillen Teilnahme an EU-Runden, einem schrittweisen Zugang zum Binnenmarkt und mehr Tempo in den Verhandlungen (mehr hier ). Die EU müsse zeigen, »dass sie erweiterungsfähig und erweiterungswillig ist«, forderte Merz damals.
Er dürfte auch heute wieder den Antreiber in Sachen EU-Erweiterung geben. Der Ehrgeiz des Kanzlers verwundert ein wenig. Schließlich fällt es der EU mit ihren 27 Mitgliedstaaten schwer genug, sich in wichtigen Fragen zu einigen.
- Mehr Hintergründe: Viele Deutsche unterschätzen laut Merz die Bedrohung durch Russland
Sachsen-Anhalt wird übersprungen
Leichter als die EU kann sich die Runde der Ministerpräsidentinnen und Ministerpräsidenten verständigen. Aber wie lange noch?
MPK-Vorsitzender Schnieder: Zweite Runde
Foto: Kay Nietfeld / dpa
Schon bald könnten dem Kreis nicht mehr nur Vertreter von Union, SPD und Grünen angehören. Sollte der AfD-Politiker Ulrich Siegmund im Dezember zum Ministerpräsidenten von Sachsen-Anhalt gewählt werden (mehr dazu hier ) und die Linke Elif Eralp in Berlin ein rot-grün-rotes Bündnis unter ihrer Führung zustande bekommen (mehr hier ), wird das die Abstimmung unter den Ländern erschweren.
Hinter den Kulissen treffen die Länderchefs Vorkehrungen dafür, dass neue Mehrheiten ihr Gremium nicht lahmlegen. Vor allem geht es um die AfD und die Sicherheitsrisiken, die von der in weiten Teilen rechtsextremen, russlandfreundlichen Partei ausgehen. Eine erste Vorsichtsmaßnahme zeigt sich heute.
Eigentlich sollte Sachsen-Anhalt in diesem Monat turnusgemäß den Vorsitz der Ministerpräsidentenkonferenz (MPK) von Rheinland-Pfalz übernehmen. Aber nach dem Wahlsieg der AfD bei der sachsen-anhaltischen Landtagswahl im September erklärte der scheidende Ministerpräsident Sven Schulze (CDU), dass sein Land darauf verzichten wolle.
Schulze behauptete, dass in der Zeit des Übergangs von einer Regierung zur nächsten »eine einwandfreie technische und inhaltliche Vorbereitung und Durchführung« der MPK nicht gewährleistet sei. Tatsächlich aber wollten der CDU-Mann und seine Länderkollegen verhindern, dass Siegmund die Runde anführt. Kurzfristig verlängerte die MPK den Vorsitz von Rheinland-Pfalz um ein Jahr. So darf auch heute wieder dessen Ministerpräsident Gordon Schnieder (CDU) die Sitzung leiten.
- Mehr Hintergründe hier: Sachsen-Anhalt setzt MPK-Vorsitz aus – Rheinland-Pfalz bleibt an Gremiumsspitze
Lesen Sie hier den aktuellen SPIEGEL-Leitartikel
- Europa muss diese Männer stoppen: Wladimir Putin plant eine unheilvolle Allianz mit Donald Trump und Xi Jinping. Die EU hat die Mittel, das zu verhindern.
Hier geht’s zum aktuellen Tagesquiz
Noch mehr Rätsel wie Viererkette, Wordle und Paarsuche finden Sie bei SPIEGEL Games.
Gewinner des Tages…
…ist Hubertus Heil. Der Sozialdemokrat hat einen Lauf. Heil bestreitet die öffentliche Debatte über die Zukunft der SPD mehr oder weniger im Alleingang. Und bringt damit sich selbst in Stellung für den Parteivorsitz.
SPD-Politiker Heil: Mann mit Ambitionen
Foto:
Marzena Skubatz / DER SPIEGEL
Interessant ist, wie Heil das macht. Der Mann sitzt seit 1998 im Bundestag, war einst Generalsekretär der SPD und Bundesarbeitsminister. Trotzdem gibt Heil jetzt den Außenseiter, den Erneuerer.
So beklagt der Niedersachse im Gespräch mit meiner Kollegin Sophie Garbe und meinem Kollegen Christoph Hickmann, dass sich die SPD zu sehr auf Sozialpolitisches verengt habe, dass sie bürokratisch und alltagsfremd daherkomme. Unter seiner Führung stünde die SPD besser da – das ist Heils Botschaft. Auch wenn er das nicht so offen sagen möchte.
- Das ganze Interview hier: »Kandidieren Sie als SPD-Chef, Herr Heil?« »Das ist möglich«
Die jüngsten Meldungen aus der Nacht
- Selenskyj möchte »so bald wie möglich« Gespräche mit USA und Russland: Russland hat einem Dreiertreffen mit den USA und der Ukraine zugestimmt. Der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj möchte schnellstmöglich mit den Gesprächen beginnen. Die russische Seite hat es offenbar weniger eilig.
- USA ziehen Botschaftspersonal aus saudi-arabischer Hauptstadt ab: Nahezu täglich greifen die Huthi-Milizen Ziele in Saudi-Arabien an – zuletzt starben zwei Menschen auf einem Ölfeld. Das US-Außenministerium reagiert nun auf die eskalierende Sicherheitslage.
- George Bushs Bruder bricht mit Tradition – und wählt demokratischen Kandidaten in Texas: Sollte es den Demokraten bei den Kongresswahlen gelingen, Texas zu erobern, wäre das ein Triumph. Kandidat James Talarico hat jetzt eine prominente Stimme bekommen: die von Langzeitrepublikaner Neil Bush.
Heute bei SPIEGEL Extra: Er wäre mit 25 fast an einem Hirntumor gestorben. Was hat das mit ihm gemacht?
Jakob Schnetz / DER SPIEGEL
Zweimal fürchtete Jan Theurich um sein Leben, dann verhalf ihm sein Neurologe zur rettenden Therapie. Warum er heute glücklicher ist .
Ich wünsche Ihnen einen guten Start in den Tag.
Ihre Marina Kormbaki, stellvertretende Leiterin des SPIEGEL-Hauptstadtbüros
description: Websites gehen wegen Sicherheitslücken offline. Der Kanzler reist an die Adria. Und die Ministerpräsidenten wappnen sich gegen die AfD. Das ist die Lage am Donnerstagmorgen.

title: Datenschutzskandal: Facebook-Konzern Meta soll Milliardenstrafe zahlen
content_c:
Cambridge-Analytica-Skandal Meta soll 25 Milliarden Dollar Strafe zahlen
Acht Jahre nach dem Skandal um den Missbrauch von Nutzerdaten ist der Facebookkonzern Meta in New Mexico zu einer Milliardenstrafe verurteilt worden. Der Fall solle anderen Tech-Unternehmen eine Warnung sein, sagte der Generalstaatsanwalt.
Der Facebook-Konzern Meta ist wegen des Datenschutz-Skandals um Cambridge Analytica zu einer Strafzahlung von 25 Milliarden Dollar verurteilt worden. Zuvor hatte eine Jury im US-Bundesstaat New Mexico festgestellt, dass der Konzern Verbraucher über den Schutz ihrer Daten getäuscht hatte.
Der Skandal um Cambridge Analytica war im März 2018 bekanntgeworden. Medien aus Großbritannien und den USA enthüllten damals, dass die britische Beratungsfirma Daten von etwa 87 Millionen Facebook-Nutzern ausgewertet hatte, ohne deren Zustimmung einzuholen. Die Daten sollen unter anderem von Politikberatern genutzt worden sein, um die Wahlen 2016 in den USA und das Brexit-Referendum im selben Jahr in Großbritannien zu beeinflussen. title: Fußball: Deutscher Trainer Hürzeler hebt in der Premier League ab
content_c:
Fußball: Deutscher Trainer Hürzeler hebt in der Premier League ab
21. Oktober 2026
"Wir lieben ihn absolut. Er ist ein unglaublicher Trainer. Die Ergebnisse sind außergewöhnlich und wir schweben derzeit förmlich", sagt Ben Parker über Fabian Hürzeler. Parker ist glühender Anhänger von Premier-League-Klub Brighton & Hove Albion und Mitherausgeber des Brightoner Fanzines "Dogma".
Da sein Lieblingsverein stark in die neue Saison gestartet ist und nach sieben Spieltagen auf Rang drei liegt, überrascht Parkers Begeisterung für den Trainer eigentlich nicht. Lobeshymnen wie diese äußern Fans vieler Vereine, die gerade einen ähnlichen Höhenflug erleben wie Brighton & Hove Albion. Doch vieles deutet darauf hin, dass Hürzeler weit mehr ist als nur eine kurzfristige Erfolgsgeschichte in der Premier League.
Hürzeler hat nie in der Fußball-Bundesliga trainiert. Nachdem er den FC St. Pauli 2024 aus der 2. Bundesliga in die höchste deutsche Spielklasse geführt hatte, wechselte er nach England. Mit 31 Jahren wurde er der jüngste Cheftrainer in der Geschichte der Premier League.
In seiner ersten Saison führte er die "Seagulls" auf Rang acht, derzeit scheint BHA noch höhere Regionen angreifen zu wollen. Der Klub hat sechs Pflichtspiele in Folge gewonnen, darunter ein 5:0 gegen den Erzrivalen Crystal Palace am vergangenen Wochenende.
Bemerkenswert: Es war die Neuauflage eines Spiels, das Hürzelers bisherigen Tiefpunkt bei Brighton markierte. Eine 0:1-Heimniederlage in der Vorsaison war damals der zehnte sieglose Auftritt in zwölf Spielen.
"Es gibt nur zwei Möglichkeiten: aufgeben oder noch härter arbeiten", sagte Hürzeler damals nach dem Spiel und kündigte an: "Und ich entscheide mich in meinem Leben immer für Letzteres."
Verhältnis zu den Fans funktioniert in beide Richtungen
Ben Parker räumt ein, dass damals längst nicht alle von Hürzeler überzeugt waren. "Nach dem Spiel gab es Unmut. Einige Fans riefen sogar: 'Morgen wirst du entlassen.'"
Doch Hürzeler habe ihm kurz nach seinem Amtsantritt erklärt, dass er genau diese Offenheit schätze. "Er sprach davon, eine Beziehung zu den Fans zu wollen, die in beide Richtungen funktioniert", erzählt Parker.
"Der Verein und er selbst sind sehr ambitioniert. Wenn die Leistungen nicht stimmen, dann sollen die Fans ihm das sagen. Genau das ist damals passiert. Ich halte das für etwas Gesundes."
Vom Amateurfußball an die Spitze
Hürzeler, der in den USA geboren wurde und als Kleinkind mit seiner Familie nach Deutschland zog, war zwar vor seiner Trainerkarriere auch aktiver Fußballer, hat aber nie auf höchstem Niveau gespielt.
Zwar lief er von der U15 bis zur U19 für deutsche Nachwuchsmannschaften auf und spielte für die zweite Mannschaft des FC Bayern München, verlor aber früh die Geduld mit dem Reserveteam-Fußball.
Im Jahr 2016 übernahm er daher mit 23 Jahren beim Fünftligisten FC Pipinsried, einem Dorfklub einige Kilometer vor den Toren von München, die Rolle als Spielertrainer. Parallel war er ab 2018 außerdem als Co-Trainer der deutschen U20-Auswahl beim Deutschen Fußballbund angestellt.
Um Geld zu verdienen arbeitete er außerdem bei einem Kunsthändler, soll diesen Job allerdings wieder verloren haben, weil er während der Arbeit zu viel Fußball guckte, statt Gemälde zu verkaufen.
Alter und fehlende Spielerkarriere kein Hindernis
Zum FC St. Pauli kam Hürzeler im Sommer 2020 - zunächst als Co-Trainer. Als Cheftrainer Timo Schultz im Dezember 2022 gefeuert wurde, rückte Hürzeler nach und nutzte diese Chance. Mit zehn Siegen in Folge stellte er einen Startrekord für die 2. Bundesliga auf. In der folgenden Saison gelang der Aufstieg.
Hürzelers ungewöhnlicher Karriereweg und einige innovative taktische Ideen während seiner Zeit bei St. Pauli führten in Deutschland zu dem Eindruck, er sei ein etwas distanzierter "Laptop-Trainer" ähnlich wie Julian Nagelsmann, dessen eigene Spielerkarriere als Profi wegen einer schweren Verletzung früh endete.
Kritiker behaupteten, einem solchen Trainer fehle die Fähigkeit, die enge Bindung und den Teamgeist zu erzeugen, die eine Mannschaft stärker machen als die Summe ihrer Einzelspieler.
Hürzeler sieht das anders: "Ich möchte ich selbst sein und keine Rolle spielen. Mein Alter hilft mir sogar dabei, die Spieler zu verstehen. Ich sage immer: Ich spreche ihre Sprache und verstehe ihre Gedanken, weil meine eigene aktive Karriere noch nicht lange zurückliegt."
Authentisch und nahbar
Auch sein temperamentvolles Auftreten an der Seitenlinie brachte ihm immer wieder Negativschlagzeilen ein. Während St. Paulis Aufstiegssaison wurde er siebenmal verwarnt. Seit seinem Wechsel zu Brighton sah er bereits neun Gelbe Karten und zusätzlich einen Platzverweis. "Emotionen gehören zum Spiel", lautet seine Erklärung dazu.
Laut Ben Parker spiegelt sich diese Authentizität auch im Alltag wider. "Für die meisten Brighton-Fans wirkt er etwas ungewöhnlich, interessant und unkonventionell. Als er kam, sprach er davon, das Establishment herauszufordern. Das passt sehr gut zu dieser Stadt."
Hürzeler sei regelmäßig an der Strandpromenade unterwegs, hole sich selbst Kaffee, fahre mit dem E-Bike statt im Wagen mit Chauffeur und habe sogar Fanveranstaltungen in Pubs organisiert und offenbar selbst bezahlt. "Er ist sehr zugänglich."
Deutsches Duo begeistert Brighton
Hürzeler ist nicht der einzige beliebte Deutsche in Brighton. Auch Pascal Groß, der im Januar von Borussia Dortmund zu BHA zurückkehrte, genießt Kultstatus. Er war zuvor bereist sieben Jahre lang in Brighton.
"Ich habe hier geheiratet und beide Kinder wurden in England geboren. Die wichtigsten Meilensteine meines Lebens haben hier stattgefunden. Ich habe meine Freunde und das Gefühl vermisst, eng mit diesem Verein verbunden zu sein."
Der Mittelfeldspieler, der nach der Fußball-Weltmeisterschaft seine Karriere in der deutschen Nationalmannschaft beendet hat, ist in der laufenden Saison einer der Erfolgsgaranten: In den ersten sieben Ligaspielen erzielte Groß drei Tore und bereitete vier weitere Treffer vor.
"Ich fühle mich sehr gut, sehr wohl. Es ist eine gute Mischung aus Fitness, Erfahrung und der Zusammenarbeit mit Fabian Hürzeler, einem Trainer, der mich so einsetzt, dass meine Stärken zur Geltung kommen", sagte Groß kürzlich in einem Interview mit dem Fußballmagazin "Kicker".
"Ich schätze ihn als Spieler sehr. Auch nachdem er den Klub verlassen hat, bin ich immer mit ihm in Kontakt geblieben", erzählte Hürzeler nach Groß' Rückkehr. "Unser Ziel damals war es, ihn zu halten. Er wollte aber seinen Traum verwirklichen. Das haben wir respektiert."
Auch bei den Fans genießt Groß ein hohes Ansehen. "Pascal Groß ist der Lieblingsspieler von praktisch allen", sagt Ben Parker. "Er ist ein sensationeller Spieler. Wegen solcher Persönlichkeiten gibt es hier eine große Sympathie für den deutschen Fußball und für Deutschland."
FC Bayern als mögliches Zukunftsziel
Groß und Hürzeler sind nur zwei Beispiele, die belegen, dass der Erfolg Brightons auf der klugen Strategie bei Trainer- und Spielerverpflichtungen unter Besitzer Tony Bloom beruht. Allerdings bedeutet das oft auch, dass erfolgreiche Akteure von größeren Vereinen umworben und erfolgreich abgeworben werden.
Chelseas Moisés Caicedo, Liverpools Alexis MacAllister und Arsenals Ben White sind nur drei Namen auf einer längeren Liste von Spielern, die in Brighton mit guten Leistungen auffielen und dann für sehr viel Geld transferiert wurden.
Parker glaubt, dass auch Brightons Trainer irgendwann zum heiß begehrten Transferobjekt werden könnte. Er sieht Hürzeler langfristig als einen Kandidaten für den FC Bayern: "Er hat selbst gesagt, dass er Bayern-Fan ist und den Klub als Maßstab für die Standards nennt, die er anstrebt. Ich könnte mir vorstellen, dass er dort in ein paar Jahren gut hineinpassen würde. Eher Bayern als Liverpool oder Chelsea."
Doch noch sieht sich Hürzeler in Brighton bestens aufgehoben. Erst kürzlich verlängerte er seinen Vertrag bis 2029. Ben Parker und den übrigen Fans von Brighton & Hove Albion soll es recht sein: "Wenn er derjenige ist, der uns den ersten großen Titel der Vereinsgeschichte bringt, dann wird er als der Größte in die Vereinsgeschichte eingehen."
Dieser Artikel wurde aus dem englischen Original "Football: German coach Hürzeler flying high in Premier League" adaptiert.
description: Seit 2024 coacht Fabian Hürzeler Brighton & Hove Albion erfolgreich in der Premier League. In Deutschland wird der Ex-Trainer des FC St. Pauli als "Laptop-Trainer" kritisch beäugt, in England wird er immer beliebter.
