Weil das Land breiten Bevölkerungsschichten zu wenige Perspektiven für ein Leben in gesicherten Verhältnissen bietet, arbeiten Millionen Rumänen im Ausland.
Vor diesem Hintergrund erstarken in Rumänien seit Längerem rechtspopulistische und rechtsextreme Parteien, darunter vor allem die prorussische, rechtsnationalistische Allianz für die Vereinigung der Rumänen (AUR). Bei der Parlamentswahl im Dezember 2024 konnte sie mehr als 18 Prozent der Stimmen gewinnen und wurde zweitstärkste Partei im Land. Außerdem sind zwei weitere Rechtsaußen-Parteien im Parlament vertreten. Zusammen verfügt das Lager über rund ein Drittel der Sitze. In aktuellen Umfragen kommt die AUR auf teils bis zu 40 Prozent und würde in einer Wahl mit großem Abstand stärkste Partei werden.
Fall der Brandmauer
Verantwortlich für diese Entwicklung ist nicht allein, aber in großem Maße, die traditionell bislang stärkste Partei, die sozialdemokratische PSD. Sie ist eine wendekommunistische Klientelpartei und wird von vielen Menschen in Rumänien als Symbol der Korruption gesehen. Sie hat sich als unfähig erwiesen, notwendige Reformen durchzuführen, und versucht seit Jahren, mit rechtspopulistisch-nationalistischen Positionen Wähler im rechten Spektrum zu gewinnen.
Die PSD war es auch, die im Frühjahr die Regierungskrise auslöste. Die vom nationalliberalen Premier Ilie Bolojan angeführte und im Sommer 2025 gebildete Vier-Parteien-Regierung hatte ernsthaft versucht, Rumäniens katastrophal hohes Haushaltsdefizit von 9,3 Prozent (2024) zu verringern und ein Sparprogramm vorgelegt.
Um sich von den unpopulären Sparmaßnahmen abzugrenzen, verließ die PSD am 20. April die Koalition und stürzte die Regierung Bolojan am 5. Mai durch ein Misstrauensvotum, gemeinsam mit den drei rechtsnationalistischen und rechtsextremen Parteien im Parlament. Es war der Fall der rumänischen Brandmauer - ein Konsens gegen rechtsextreme und antieuropäische Kräfte, den Rumäniens gemäßigt konservativer Staatspräsident Nicusor Dan im Sommer 2025 initiiert hatte.
Durchhangeln bis zur Wahl
Auch das jetzige Krisenende steht im Zeichen von Parteipolitik. Der Staatspräsident Nicusor Dan hatte damit gedroht, das Parlament aufzulösen, wenn seine vierte Nominierung eines Premierministers seit dem Zerbrechen der Bolojan-Regierung keine Mehrheit finden würde. Das hätte vorgezogene Neuwahlen bedeutet. Daran hat im Augenblick, mit einer Ausnahme, keine Partei des nicht-extremistischen Spektrums im Parlament ein Interesse. Lediglich die grün-liberale Union Rettet Rumänien (USR) trat dafür ein.
Demgegenüber wird die PSD mit der Regierung Niculescu versuchen, sich durch Klientelpolitik bis zur nächsten Parlamentswahl Ende 2028 durchzuhangeln. Ähnliches gilt für die Ungarn-Partei UDMR, die ebenfalls als äußerst korrupt gilt, aber von vielen Wählern der ungarischen Minderheit Rumäniens als alternativlos gesehen wird. Die PNL wiederum versucht, als liberale und vergleichsweise reformentschlossene Partei, vor allem proeuropäische Wähler aus der rumänischen Mittelschicht anzusprechen. Sie konkurriert dabei mit der grün-liberalen USR.
Der Handlungsspielraum des neuen Premiers ist angesichts dieser Umstände eingeschränkt. Nach seiner Wahl am Dienstag appellierte Luca Niculescu, der als Staatssekretär zuletzt Rumäniens geplanten Beitritt zur OECD verhandelte, an alle Unterstützer der Koalition: "Es gibt viele Probleme, die dringend gelöst werden müssen. Rumänien kann nicht mehr warten."
Rumänische Beobachter bezweifeln jedoch, dass er erhört wird. Der Politologe Sorin Ionita schrieb in einem Beitrag für das rumänische Portal Contributors: "Luca Niculescu wird zwar formal die Regierung führen, doch bestehen keine Illusionen, dass er die PSD zu irgendetwas bewegen könnte." Ähnlich sieht es der Politologe Cristian Pirvulescu. Die meisten wichtigen Entscheidungen, so Pirvulescu, würden auf einen Zeitpunkt nach der Wahl 2028 verschoben werden.

title: Тарифи на газ від 1 листопада: що зміниться в платіжках українців і до чого слід підготуватися
content_c:
Тарифи на газ від 1 листопада: що зміниться в платіжках українців і до чого слід підготуватися
Попри збереження стандартної вартості кубометра, у листопаді підсумкові витрати українців на газ можуть виявитися набагато вищими, ніж очікувалося.
Від 1 листопада 2026 року вартість блакитного палива для побутових клієнтів «Нафтогазу» залишиться на рівні 7,96 гривні за кубометр. Компанія зафіксувала цей тариф до кінця квітня 2027 року, тож сам по собі початок опалювального сезону не спричинить зростання ціни за газ.
Про це повідомляють на сайті газорозподільчої компанії.
Втім, у зимовий період підсумкові суми в квитанціях суттєво зростуть, адже витрати повністю залежатимуть від реальних обсягів споживання на обігрів житла.
Скільки коштуватиме кубометр і як діє тариф
У листопаді побутові споживачі «Нафтогазу» отримають рахунки за звичною ціною. Згідно з інформацією на офіційному сайті постачальника, тарифний план «Фіксований» діє від 1 травня 2026 року до 30 квітня 2027 року включно.
Вартість становить 7,96 грн за кубометр із урахуванням ПДВ. Таким чином, сам по собі старт опалювального періоду не призведе до здорожчання одиниці палива. Водночас варто враховувати: інші приватні газопостачальники в Україні мають право встановлювати власні цінники в межах чинного законодавства.
Скільки доведеться платити українцям за газ узимку
Сума в щомісячній квитанції напряму залежить від кількості спожитих кубометрів. За фіксованої ціни 7,96 грн за кубометр орієнтовні витрати виглядатимуть так:
- при споживанні 10 кубометрів на місяць платіжка становитиме 79,60 грн;
- за 50 кубометрів доведеться віддати 398 грн;
- якщо домогосподарство витрачає 100 кубометрів, сума сягне 796 грн;
- за 150 кубометрів доведеться заплатити 1 194 грн;
- за 200 кубометрів доведеться заплатити 1 592 грн;
- у випадку високого споживання на рівні 300 кубометрів витрати становитимуть 2 388 грн;
- 500 кубометрів обійдуться у 3 980 грн.
Це орієнтовні приклади розрахунку, а не затверджені норми. Реальне споживання залежить від площі будинку або квартири, якості утеплення, енергоефективності обладнання та чисельності мешканців.
Сім’я, яка використовує газ винятково для приготування їжі на плиті, витрачає в рази менше за тих, хто обігріває житло газовим котлом.
Окрема плата за доставку газу: що треба знати
У комунальних рахунках важливо чітко розрізняти дві окремі послуги: постачання газу та його розподіл.
Постачання — це плата за безпосередньо використаний обсяг палива за ціною 7,96 грн/м³. Розподіл (доставка) — це послуга місцевого оператора газорозподільних мереж, який утримує трубопроводи та транспортує газ до оселі.
Вартість доставки розраховується за окремими тарифами регулятора, які залежать від регіону та замовленої річної потужності. Саме тому підсумкові суми у двох різних родинах можуть відрізнятися навіть за однакового обсягу споживання.
До якого числа потрібно заплатити за газ
Оплачувати спожитий газ необхідно щомісяця до 25-го числа за попередній період. Зокрема, рахунок за листопад слід закрити до 25 грудня 2026 року.
Аби уникнути заборгованостей чи помилкових нарахувань, вкрай важливо вчасно передавати показання лічильника — щомісяця від 1-го до 5-го числа. Якщо дані не надати вчасно, обсяг визначать за середньорозрахунковими нормами, що іноді призводить до розбіжностей у платіжках.
Збереження субсидій і пільг
Отримувачі житлових субсидій та державних пільг продовжують обслуговуватися за фіксованим тарифом. Наявність тарифного плану «Фіксований» жодним чином не позбавляє громадян права на соціальну допомогу від держави.
Підсумковий розмір субсидії розраховується за стандартною процедурою на основі доходів сім’ї, її складу та діючих соціальних нормативів.
Чому уряд не підвищує ціну на газ
Рішення про збереження пільгових цін для населення та виробників тепла ухвалено на урядовому рівні. Спеціальні умови постачання газу продовжено до 31 березня 2027 року.
Кабінет Міністрів України керується діючим мораторієм на підвищення окремих комунальних тарифів на час воєнного стану, а також прагне підтримати громадян у складних соціально-економічних умовах.
Комуналка в Україні 2026 — останні новини
Українцям мають повернути майже 93 млн грн через порушення в тарифах на житлово-комунальні послуги. Від початку року перевірили 140 підприємств і знайшли порушення майже у дев’яти з десяти, тож компанії мають перерахувати тарифи та сплатити штрафи.
У 2026 році учасники бойових дій можуть отримати 75% знижки на оплату житла й комунальних послуг у межах норм, без урахування доходів сім’ї. Для цього треба звернутися до Пенсійного фонду України із заявою та документами.
Підписуйтесь на наші канали у Telegram та Viber.

title: Диалог с Кремлем: Европа ищет главного переговорщика по Украине — Politico
content_c:
В европейских правительствах всё чаще признают, что в ближайшее время им, возможно, придётся выбрать представителя для прямых переговоров с российским диктатором Владимиром Путиным по поводу мирного соглашения для Украины. В то же время главным вопросом остается то, кто согласится взять на себя эту сложную и рискованную миссию, пишет Politico.
Отмечается, что необходимость для Европы определиться с возможным представителем для переговоров с Россией стала особенно актуальной после того, как специальный посланник президента США Стив Уиткофф посетил Москву. Там он должен был предложить Путину провести совместный саммит с участием главы Белого дома Дональда Трампа и президента Украины Владимира Зеленского, чтобы достичь договоренности о прекращении огня.
В то же время президент Чехии Петр Павел во вторник подчеркнул, что российский лидер не воспринимает Европейский Союз как авторитетную сторону. По словам Павела, Путин отказывается общаться с председателем Еврокомиссии Урсулой фон дер Ляйен и главой дипломатии ЕС Каей Каллас, а также прекратил контакты с другими европейскими лидерами, в числе которых президент Франции Эммануэль Макрон.
«ЕС должен определить человека или группу людей, которые будут выступать от имени Европы. Это не обязательно должны быть представители ЕС или НАТО, а просто лидеры, которым другие предоставят полномочия вести переговоры», — сказал президент Чехии.
Politico отмечает, что последние шаги Трампа вызвали беспокойство в Украине и среди её европейских партнёров. Американский президент обсуждает условия урегулирования войны без учета их позиции и все чаще склоняется к поддержке России в войне, которая длится уже почти пять лет.
На этом фоне в Брюсселе и других европейских столицах вновь заговорили о необходимости наладить прямой диалог с Кремлем. Собственный канал связи с Москвой помог бы Европе защищать свои интересы, а Украине тем временем дал бы возможность противостоять попыткам навязать ей несправедливые условия мирного соглашения.
«Как бы это ни было неприятно, я действительно считаю, что наличие какого-то канала связи с Путиным было бы полезным. Я не очень оптимистичен в отношении того, что это даст какие-то существенные результаты в краткосрочной перспективе, но иметь канал, которым можно будет воспользоваться, когда представится возможность, — это неплохо», — сказал почетный научный сотрудник Королевского объединенного института оборонных исследований в Лондоне Дэвид Лидингтон.
Однако среди дипломатов и представителей правительств до сих пор нет единого мнения относительно того, кто лучше всего мог бы вести переговоры от имени Европы. Издание пишет, что среди возможных кандидатов — Урсула фон дер Ляйен, которая ранее непосредственно обсуждала с Трампом торговые вопросы, а также председатель Европейского совета Антониу Кошта, чей офис ранее наладил канал связи с Кремлем. Еще одним претендентом может стать Каллас, которая представляет общие интересы европейских стран.
Так, дипломат одной из стран ЕС считает, что европейские чиновники должны понять, что договоренности между Путиным и Трампом не будут зависеть от правил и процедур Евросоюза. Он подчеркнул, что Европа не может отправить на переговоры двух или трех представителей, каждый из которых будет выступать от имени ЕС. Также, по его словам, при выборе того, кто будет представлять объединение, нужно руководствоваться тем, какой вариант будет наиболее выгодным для Европы, а не личными амбициями или борьбой за власть.
Politico также пишет, что одним из возможных кандидатов на роль представителя Европы является президент Финляндии Александр Стубб, который находится вне институтов ЕС. В его пользу говорят два фактора. Он, вероятно, имеет лучшие отношения с Трампом среди лидеров Евросоюза, а Финляндия обладает многолетним опытом взаимодействия с Россией. Страны имеют общую границу протяженностью 1 300 километров и в прошлом воевали друг с другом.
Дипломат отметил, что Стубб привлекает внимание благодаря опыту Финляндии и её длительному диалогу с Россией. Он добавил, что финны лучше других европейцев понимают, что нужно для обеспечения безопасности в таких условиях.
Другой дипломат ЕС считает, что Стубб на данный момент является единственным, кто предложил конкретную инициативу и продемонстрировал готовность взять на себя политическую ответственность. По его мнению, президент Финляндии мог бы представлять Европу на предстоящем мирном саммите.
Еще один европейский дипломат подчеркнул, что во время предстоящих мирных переговоров по Украине важно обеспечить представительство всего Евросоюза, а не только нескольких влиятельных стран, в частности Германии, Франции и Великобритании.
Четвертый дипломат ЕС рассказал, что во время саммита в Брюсселе на прошлой неделе европейские лидеры поинтересовались у Кошты, стоит ли ему уже провести беседу с Владимиром Путиным. Однако тот ответил, что пока не планирует общаться с российским лидером.
«Но Кошта должен начать разговор с Путиным, если мы хотим играть определенную роль в переговорах. Отказываясь от диалога, мы играем на руку нашим противникам», — сказал дипломат.
Он также считает, что Кошта лучше подходит на роль представителя ЕС, чем Урсула фон дер Ляйен и Каллас. По его мнению, оба политика слишком активно поддерживают Украину, чтобы эффективно представлять весь Евросоюз на переговорах на высшем уровне. В частности, Каллас открыто критиковала Трампа. Дипломат добавил, что Кошта мог бы быть более беспристрастным посредником.
Ранее издание The Wall Street Journal писало, что во время телефонного разговора 9 октября Путин предложил провести в следующем месяце встречу с участием президента США и лидера Китая Си Цзиньпина, на которой хочет обсудить ситуацию в Украине и добиться соглашения о завершении войны на условиях, выгодных для Москвы. Пресс-секретарь Кремля Дмитрий Песков подтвердил журналистам, что стороны продолжают обсуждать возможную встречу, однако пока не определились, состоится ли она и какие вопросы планируют рассмотреть.
После этого министр иностранных дел Украины Андрей Сибига заявил, что без участия Украины эта трехсторонняя встреча лишь подтолкнет Путина к продолжению войны против Украины. Он отметил, что приглашение Путина на такую встречу лишь подпитает его манию величия и придаст ему вес, которого он не заслуживает.
Между тем, комментируя сообщения СМИ о предложении Путина провести трехстороннюю встречу с лидерами США и Китая для обсуждения завершения войны против Украины, представители Еврокомиссии подчеркнули, что любые договоренности должны уважать территориальную целостность Украины. Они также отметили, что Европа должна играть важную роль в предстоящих переговорах.

title: Кількість постраждалих внаслідок нічної атаки на Київ зросла до 15, серед них двоє дітей
content_c:
Внаслідок ворожого обстрілу Києва в ніч на 22 жовтня постраждали 15 людей, серед них двоє 15-річних дітей, повідомив міський голова Віталій Кличко.
"8 поранених перебувають у стаціонарах міських лікарень", – написав він у Telegram у четвер.
За його даними, у Печерському районі пошкоджено будівлю станції швидкої допомоги, а також шість автомобілів швидкої", – написав він.
"Серед медпрацівників постраждалих немає", – зазначив Кличко.
Джерело: https://t.me/vitaliy_klitschko/7955

title: US embassy accuses Canada of election meddling ahead of midterms
content_c:
US embassy accuses Canada of election meddling ahead of midterms
- Published
The US Embassy in Ottawa has accused Canadian officials of election meddling ahead of the November midterms.
The embassy said Canadian leaders have brushed off concerns over "potential interference", and that ministers and premiers "openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances".
Canadian leaders, including Prime Minister Mark Carney, have dismissed the claims. Relations between the North American neighbours have hardened during second Trump administration.
The midterms will determine which political party controls both branches of the US Congress, which could have a significant impact on the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.
The fact sheet released by the US Embassy on Wednesday alleges the Canadian government "brushes off concerns about potential interference in U.S. elections, even as its ministers and premiers openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances".
It cites comments and actions, like meetings with US Democrats and calling for retaliatory tariffs against the US.
For example, it says that when Industry Minister Mélanie Joly was asked what she expected regarding tariffs if Democrats were to win midterm elections, she responded, "That's exactly why I'm meeting so many governors and potential presidential candidates."
Ontario Premier Doug Ford pushed Canada's federal government, it states, to consider additional retaliatory tariffs on imports from "politically significant states to the current administration's base of support".
Asked on Wednesday about the allegations, Carney noted that it was the US that first initiated trade actions against Canada.
"We've responded to those to protect Canadian jobs, to protect Canadian companies and develop our economy," Carney said.
He said his government's response has been "in the interests of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy".
Carney, who was announcing a nearly C$9bn ($6.2bn) aid package in response to US tariffs, was accompanied by both Joly and Ford.
Ford said that he has "no interest at all" in interfering in US elections.
"I'll tell you what the American people want. They want certainty, they want stability," Ford said, adding that he will focus on Ontario and Canada.
"The people of the United States will make that determination in the midterms," he said.
Last week, Minister Joly denied Canadian interference and said that Canadians "never accept that also being done to us in Canada", according to CBC.
She said that her recent visits to the US were "to attract investments" from American companies, which she plans to continue.
- What are the US midterms? A simple guide 
  - Published6 October
Washington and Ottawa have argued for months over tariffs and trade, which once flowed freely across their borders, and the effects of Canada's counter measures.
Earlier this month, US Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra warned that US officials are "closely watching" Canada's politicians for signs of election interference.
Trump administration officials have also been accused of making inappropriate remarks about the separation referendum in the province of Alberta this week.
A petition calling for Hoekstra's removal from his post for "undermining the Canada-U.S. diplomatic relations" has received more than 280,000 signatures.
  - Published1 day ago

Chris Mason: Jackdaw approved but tricky energy trade-offs remain
- Published
The decision to grant approval for drilling at the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea and the further delay in a decision about the Rosebank oil field, also in the North Sea, are case studies in the slow-motion awkwardness the UK has collectively had, over years, about energy.
At the heart of that awkwardness, these questions: where should our energy come from, and with what costs and consequences, for the customer and for the environment?
Since becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham has talked about a desire to be "pragmatic" about the North Sea as he puts it, which is why this decision about Jackdaw isn't a surprise.
In fact it felt near inevitable after President Trump blurted out – after his first phone call with Burnham in the summer – that the prime minister had told him he would "open up the North Sea".
Burnham acknowledged the two leaders had discussed the issue, arguing: "There is a resource there. When people are struggling - you can't ignore that."
What we now know is the government is approving drilling of the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea, about 150 miles east of Aberdeen.
A decision on Rosebank, an oil field about 80 miles north east of Shetland, is expected to take a bit longer.
The timeline of back and forth about both projects is worth revisiting. Jackdaw was first approved four years ago, Rosebank three years ago.
But after a legal challenge by environmental campaigners, it was ruled that consent had been granted unlawfully and there needed to be a more detailed assessment of the environmental impact.
And then, of course – there is politics, international and domestic, between parties and within parties.
Debate about energy security and spiralling prices, given the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, the environmental impact, carbon emissions and the message new drilling sends to the wider world.
But others point to the extra carbon emissions when energy is imported, the tax revenues generated from domestic energy and the social and economic consequences of the British oil and gas sector deindustrialising too quickly and, in particular, the impact on cities such as Aberdeen.
Then, for the government, there are the promises the Labour Party made when it was seeking your support at the general election in 2024.
Page 52 of Labour's manifesto reads like a rhetorical twister – a paragraph of promises seeking to stretch in multiple directions at the same time, trying to keep a breadth of people happy simultaneously, or perhaps not annoy too many people too much.
"Labour will not revoke existing licences and we will partner with business and workers to manage our existing fields for the entirety of their lifespan. Crucially, oil and gas production in the North Sea will be with us for decades to come, and the North Sea will be managed in a way that does not jeopardise jobs," it reads.
"And our offshore workers will lead the world in the industries of the future. We will not issue new licences to explore new fields because they will not take a penny off bills, cannot make us energy secure, and will only accelerate the worsening climate crisis," it adds.
Crucially, the Jackdaw and Rosebank licences had already been issued, leaving political wriggle room on these two outstanding and high profile decisions the Labour government inherited on taking office.
But the multiple trade-offs, of course, remain very real, including for some of the key individuals involved.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who used to be the energy secretary, has long been vocal about what he sees as the need to move away from fossil fuels.
His successor, Miatta Fahnbulleh, who has announced this decision, previously wrote, external that "to have a shot at staying within 1.5C global warming, we can't have any new oil or gas fields," adding "it's irresponsible and short sighted to be funding new fossil fuels when we need to get to Net Zero fast."
Fahnbulleh has today told BBC Radio Scotland gas from Jackdaw will be "in our homes and businesses this month" but acknowledged that it "won't lower our energy bills this winter".
Instead, she is grounding her argument for approving this in energy security and saying the tax revenue generated will go into an "Energy Wealth Fund" to pay for "low carbon and renewable projects".
Rosebank, she added, was a "different proposition" as its oil would be exported, but she will "look at it".
Politically, the decision on Jackdaw is considerably easier for the government than the decision on Rosebank.
Broadly speaking, most Labour MPs are comfortable with endorsing Jackdaw. It is also a project backed by the Conservatives and Reform (who argue a decision should have been taken much sooner) and the Scottish National Party and the Liberal Democrats. The Green Party of England and Wales are opposed.
On Rosebank, the argument is much more contentious within the Labour Party. Some, who can see the rationale for Jackdaw cannot see it for Rosebank. Bluntly, it is a much more difficult decision, as Fahnbulleh has acknowledged.
What we can expect in the coming hours and days - as it has started already - is a resumption of all the arguments these projects have already provoked, with some saying approval should have happened ages ago, alongside plenty more.
And others arguing the announcement is utterly irresponsible.

title: Putin orders release of jailed American as he meets Trump envoy for Ukraine talks
content_c:
Vladimir Putin ordered the release of an American man from a Russian jail as he met Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg on Wednesday for fresh talks on ending the war in Ukraine, amid increasingly close relations between Moscow and Washington.
Trump had previously asked Putin to free Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old former teacher who had spent more than four years in Russian jails on charges of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine.
His release appeared to be Moscow’s latest calculated move to bring Trump further into line with Putin’s position on Ukraine, while offering the US president a diplomatic victory before the midterm elections.
Hubbard was released unilaterally by Russia, rather than as part of a prisoner exchange as has often been the case with previous releases of Americans held in the country.
Writing on social media after the release was announced, Trump said it followed a request he had made “directly” to Putin last week.
He wrote on Truth Social: “The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return – an unprecedented situation for Russia … There was no ‘swap’ necessary for this release.”
Hubbard’s younger sister told the Associated Press she had spoken to her brother, who said he had thought he was “going to die in prison”.
“He’s out of Russia territory. He is free, praise God,” Patricia Hubbard Fox said, adding that her brother suffered beatings and starvation while he was held captive.
Witkoff, meanwhile, lavished praise on Putin during their meeting at the grand Constantine Palace in St Petersburg, describing the Russian president as a humanitarian.
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Witkoff told Putin. He also conveyed Trump’s thanks for a deal to resume Russian diesel exports to the US.
The Russian president is wanted by the international criminal court (ICC) as a war criminal, in relation to the deportation of Ukrainian children to Russia during the war.
More than 17,500 civilians have been confirmed killed in Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to the UN, which says the true toll is likely to be significantly higher.
The warmth of Witkoff’s remarks stood in stark contrast to the increasingly hostile rhetoric directed at Volodymyr Zelenskyy by senior US officials, most notably Trump, who has called for the Ukrainian president to resign and portrayed him as the main obstacle to peace.
Witkoff travelled to Russia from Oslo, where he had met Zelenskyy and European leaders a day earlier in an attempt to inject momentum into stalled negotiations, with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine now in its fifth year.
Witkoff told Putin during a televised portion of their meeting: “We’ve brought some papers. It’s really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you’ll read that at your leisure.”
The visit was Witkoff’s ninth to Russia since Trump tasked him with brokering an end to the war.
Witkoff described his meeting with Putin as “constructive” but said “important work” remained and trilateral talks between the US, Russia and Ukraine “at the technical level” would follow.
The Kremlin said it had agreed “in principle” to the talks, which would focus on how to guarantee the security of Ukraine and Russia once the war ended.
The latest rupture in relations between Washington and Kyiv was triggered by Trump’s surprise decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel as part of a deal with Putin, followed by his call for Zelenskyy to be replaced after Ukraine refused to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Kyiv has since complained of disruptions to US intelligence-sharing and restrictions on its access to Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite network.
Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that Washington had resumed providing advance warnings of Russian missile attacks after his meeting with Witkoff in Oslo.
But Ukraine continues to face restrictions on Starshield, although it remains unclear who ordered them. The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk had personally ordered the slowdown, while Reuters, citing sources, said the directive had come from inside the White House.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said on Wednesday that the decision to restrict Ukraine’s access came from Musk.
“I’m not aware that we knew about this decision beforehand. But that’s irrelevant,” Rubio told reporters during a trip to India.
“The bottom line is that, that is governed by a private commercial contract as to how their stuff can be used and what speeds they’ll allow it to be used at.”
During Wednesday’s meeting with Witkoff, Putin thanked Trump and his wife, Melania, for “their attention to efforts to end the war”.
Yet there are few signs of an imminent breakthrough. Despite repeated Ukrainian calls for a ceasefire, including a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure, Moscow has given little indication that it intends to end its bombardment of Ukraine as winter approaches, apparently confident that continued pressure will help it extract greater concessions from Kyiv.
The Russian leader remains intent on sticking to his maximalist war aims, including his demand for full Russian control of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region.
Putin also sought to emphasise the prospects for closer economic ties between Russia and the US once the war ends, suggesting that Moscow could significantly increase its exports of fertilisers to the American market.
Russian officials said the first tanker carrying diesel to the US would depart on Thursday as part of an initial shipment of about 300,000 tonnes.
Energy analysts and traders have questioned whether Trump’s agreement to temporarily resume Russian diesel imports will deliver meaningful relief to US consumers before the midterm elections, arguing that the volumes involved are too small to significantly ease the global supply squeeze.
The talks on Wednesday also touched on a possible meeting in China next month between Putin, Trump and the Chinese president, Xi Jinping. The Kremlin said Beijing was already making preparations for what it described as an unprecedented summit between the three leaders.

title: Everyone hates Oxford Street. Will pedestrianisation save it?
content_c:
In February, the mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, announced that Britain’s best-known thoroughfare, Oxford Street, would be pedestrianised. To the surprise of every Londoner that I have spoken to in the past few months, it is actually happening. On Monday 26 October, the busiest shopping street in Europe – or, precisely, half of its 1.2-mile stretch – will be closed to traffic, putting an end to several decades of bitter arguments, obstructions and delays. Cars, lorries, vans, taxis, buses, bicycles, ebikes, scooters will be banned. Nothing but pedestrians (and emergency vehicles) will be allowed in.
This change will mark the most remarkable transformation to the streetscape of central London since at least 2003, when Trafalgar Square was turned from a glorified roundabout into one of London’s most recognisable public spaces. It will also form the most visible part of the mayor’s legacy, whether or not Khan runs for a fourth term in 2028. Three years ago, Khan published a memoir and manifesto, Breathe, attributing his asthma to growing up inhaling London’s polluted air. For the mayor, pedestrianising Oxford Street is the culmination of a mission to create a greener city that is oriented around public health, walking and cycling.
Pedestrianisation is one thing; making Oxford Street somewhere anyone actually wants to spend time is another. For weary Londoners and anxious visitors alike, it is a headache in the form of a high street. Its primary associations are crowds, stress, dirt, noise, the tackiest incarnations of consumer capitalism, and crime. At one point during my research I approached a harried police officer in the throng outside Tottenham Court Road tube station and asked if she thought pedestrianisation would be good for Oxford Street, or make her job harder. Both, she said.
This is not to say Oxford Street is an empty, dying high street. At the last count, it receives more than 500,000 visitors every day – equivalent to the population of Edinburgh. It seems reasonable to assume that most of London’s 22 million annual foreign visitors set foot on it at some point. The street generates 5% of the capital’s economic output, and lives in the national imagination the way few others do. “When I was 17, London meant Oxford Street,” sang Everything But the Girl, in their 1988 song of the same name: “It was a little world.” And yet, nobody loves Oxford Street. During the course of writing this article, I haven’t met anyone who will even admit to liking it.
On a Sunday evening in September, I did something I had always carefully avoided doing before and cycled its full length. Even at the end of the weekend, it was overwhelming – with teenagers careening on rented ebikes and gaudy pedicabs parked in the middle of the pavement, blaring music. The pavements were thick with people, in part because the road was still thick with traffic. On another occasion, I watched a late-middle-aged woman perch awkwardly outside Ikea on a narrow black electricity box, in the absence of anywhere else to rest. For most Londoners, Oxford Street is a necessary evil, to be visited with surgical precision before fleeing the scene: a site of crime, grime and perhaps some Christmas shopping. “Who,” wondered the FT’s architecture critic in 2020, “lingers any longer than they have to in London’s worst thoroughfare?”
The grime itself is no joke. In the 1990s, when Oxford Street was known for its huge record shops such as HMV and Virgin Megastore, I remember returning to my south London home on the tube, blowing my nose and seeing a tissue full of jet-black snot. Its narrow streetway and tall buildings on either side create an “urban canyon”, trapping the heavy diesel fumes emanating from its buses and taxis (private car access has been restricted since 1972). In 2014, it was found to have the highest concentration of nitrogen dioxide pollution in the world. In the same year, the crime had become so bad that the United Arab Emirates warned its citizens to avoid the area for their own safety.
Since then it has become better known for its lawbreaking small businesses, where substantial raids have hauled in counterfeit goods and illegal vapes. This decade has seen the rise of mysterious US candy stores and empty souvenir shops that allegedly thrive thanks to tax evasion. Covid and internet shopping hit Oxford Street hard: vacancy levels soared from 4.5% in 2019 to 16.9% by early 2023, and it was often these businesses that filled the gaps. The current Google Street View images of its shopfronts, taken just two years ago, already look like a postcard from the past.
That Oxford Street has been struggling hurts the reputation of London as a whole. This is in tabloid parlance, “the nation’s high street”, home to the flagship branches of iconic department stores alongside global retail brands. Khan’s gamble is that the pedestrianisation can reverse what he conceded in 2024 was a case of “managed decline”, and will flood the street with life again.
In the offices of East, near London Fields, Julian Lewis and Archie Bashford were seated around a 4ft-long cardboard model of Oxford Street and talking animatedly about bollards. Lewis and his team are public realm architects, devoted not to buildings, but the world beyond them: signage, benches, perches, kerbs, paving, lighting, planters, trees and public art. East have carried out nearly 30 high street redesign projects in as many years, but this is the big one.
The first thing Lewis’s team did after being awarded the contract last year was to dive into the archives. The starting point was a little-known 1932 article in Good Housekeeping by Virginia Woolf. For Woolf, Oxford Street appeared as a “great rolling ribbon … the pebbly bed of a river … washed by a bright stream”. She saw it as gaudy, but also sparkling, thrilling and overwhelming, defined by the restless movement of its messy public. (Her essay also shows us how weird the street has long been – in 1932, it was apparently full of hawkers selling live tortoises.) It was these riverine characteristics that became the starting point for the thousands of material, small-scale design decisions that East are making. The “play of light on surfaces, the subtle reflectivity of a bench or a column” can all help bring out those tendencies, Bashford told me.
The pedestrianisation happening next week will cover 0.6 miles, stretching westwards from close to the Oxford Circus crossing to Selfridges. (Sadiq Khan has expressed his commitment to eventually pedestrianise all 1.2 miles of the street.) The most noticeable transformation will be how much greener it is becoming. The architects’ plan is to experiment with introducing young trees in pots, alongside new places to sit. They will use the test phase – which will last from next week until spring 2027 – to learn about how people respond to the trees. Will they become meeting points? Rest stops? Landmarks for wayfinding? Ideally they will provide respite, Lewis said, “a refuge from the flow of people, which is the river analogy again – maybe that’s optimistic, but instilling some relative calm”.
The pedestrianised zone’s edges will be marked by bollards. Lewis has strong opinions on this subject, and speaks about bollards as if they were people. “Bollards are generally horrible things,” he told me. Too often they seem “apologetic”, he said. “A misaligned, plasticky reflective strip [on a bollard] sends the message: ‘Sorry, I didn’t really mean to be here, but I need to let you know there are some vehicles nearby.’ Instead, they should be saying: ‘I’m happy to be here, because I’m doing a job.’”
An abundance of considerations go into designing the right kind of bollard, including security, maintenance, aesthetics, accessibility, climate, foot traffic, crowd flow and civic pride. Oxford Street’s bollards have to be exactly 1.2 metres apart, for reasons of HVM – hostile vehicle mitigation – but they also need to be helpful and use “the existing language of the street”. They will be made of ductile iron, because it is more resilient than cast iron: it’s springy, and doesn’t crack when you hit it. They are also matt, because shiny bollards are too flashy, and detract from the ambience. “They’re very sophisticated,” Lewis said, and he meant it.
One of the project’s primary ambitions is to better integrate Oxford Street with its neighbours. It is surrounded by four areas with strikingly different identities: Soho, Fitzrovia, Mayfair and Marylebone. “There’s this slightly numb connection to Oxford Street itself, like: where the hell is Oxford Street? It might as well not be there, with regard to the relationship with these incredible centres,” Lewis said. “People want to go to Soho. They want to go to Marylebone. People live in Fitzrovia. Oxford Street does not have a place yet, it’s a non-spatial space, which is unbelievable given how famous it is.”
This is where landscape architecture and design comes in. The noun the architects use over and over is “invitation” – how do you encourage people to do the unthinkable, and linger in the newly pedestrianised space, and move freely in and out of it? The built environment has to invite them to do so. One innovation Lewis’s team wants to explore is outdoor public dining – not outdoor tables for restaurants, because there are barely any on Oxford Street, but continental-style tables to sit and eat whatever you want; takeaway food bought in Soho, or a packed lunch you made at home. “The idea of sitting there having sandwiches at a picnic bench, next to a shop in which you can buy a Prada handbag, is a fantastic kind of paradox,” Lewis said with a smile. “And it’s also very London.”
To understand where the idea of pedestrianising Oxford Street came from, you need to acquaint yourself with the work of a Danish urban planner called Jan Gehl. In 2003, when Ken Livingstone was mayor of London, Gehl was asked to spend 18 months researching the flaws in London’s streetscape, and in June 2004 he produced a 120-page report entitled Towards a Fine City for People. Gehl thought there was a huge amount of work to be done. “London comes only after Moscow in the contempt the city planners show for pedestrians,” he said that year. “You never see any children on London streets – what have you done with them all?” The answer is that they have been increasingly shut indoors: driven everywhere in cars or not trusted to play outside – compared both with earlier generations of Londoners, and with most other children across Europe.
Gehl wanted to transform the capital into one of the world’s most walking-friendly cities by 2015. But with the 2004 mayoral election taking place the same month, the radical edges of the final report that was published by Livingstone’s City Hall were sanded down. There have been many experiments in recent decades to bring social life back to Oxford Street: tweaks to crossings, traffic restrictions and pavements, and, largely to accommodate more shopping, from 2005 to 2012, one single traffic-free day in the run-up to Christmas called Very Important Pedestrians Day.
One thing everyone agrees on is that a dramatic transformation is long overdue. By the time Khan replaced Boris Johnson as mayor in 2016, London had fallen behind cities such as Paris, Barcelona and Berlin when it came to infrastructure for cyclists and pedestrians, and measures to curb car numbers. There are two big structural changes sweeping through the great cities of western Europe that have also shaped Khan’s ability to finally get this done. The first is that the motorcar is no longer king in the modern city. The second is that shopping has been displaced. Even though Oxford Street remains a river bobbing with more than 20 flagship stores, maximal spending is no longer the only consideration. In the age of same-day delivery, out-of-town fulfilment centres, and peer-to-peer secondhand marketplaces such as Vinted, what should replace shopping at the heart of the modern city?

On our walk, the first signs of change were visible: the concrete bases of the new bollards were in place and the old wooden planters – “really poorly designed”, in Khan’s view – had had their dying shrubs removed. Outside the flagship UK store of the US shoe brand Vans, which styles itself as not merely a skateboarding attire shop, but “a space to express yourself” and a “cultural hub”, Khan spoke with gusto about the so-called experience economy.
In city centres post-Covid, there is “this desire, particularly among young people, for human connection,” he said, gesturing through the open concertina doors of the Vans shop, where a full drum kit, guitar and amps had been set up, facing out on to the street. “When you can buy almost anything you want, what’s the one thing that you can’t buy? That proximity to someone else and having that human experience.”
Given that everyone agrees Oxford Street needs overhauling, why has this taken so long? “The West End doesn’t have a single owner,” Khan said. “There are two local authorities, a transport authority, a strategic authority, five business improvement districts, hundreds of businesses and some major landowners.” The maestro trying to conduct this unruly orchestra is now the OSDC, which was created by the mayor. While reporting this story, I noticed the OSDC sought to keep an iron grip on press coverage. Perhaps this is because the local politics around Oxford Street have been fiercely contested for so long.
In fact, angst over vehicle traffic on Oxford Street is about as old as London’s mayor. In 1971, when Sadiq Khan was a baby, so many pedestrians were spilling from overcrowded pavements into the road and being hit by cars that an Oxford Street Action Committee was formed. During one protest calling for cars to be banned, 22 people were arrested. The Greater London Council introduced the first ban of private cars (between 7am and 7pm) the following year, marking the beginning of 50 years of gradual traffic restrictions.
Full pedestrianisation has faced decades of opposition and obstruction, primarily from the Conservative-run Westminster council – continuing when Labour took it over from 2022 to 2026 – but also from taxi drivers, disabled access groups, local residents, smaller traders and local neighbourhood groups such as the Soho Society and Mayfair Forum. The latter worry that plans to reroute buses, delivery lorries and taxis into quiet conservation areas surrounding the street will “destroy” those areas, as Tim Lord of the Soho Society put it. Accessibility advocates and the Licensed Taxi Drivers’ Association argue that pedestrianisation will create a transport desert for older people and disabled visitors. (In a statement, the OSDC admitted that journeys to Oxford Street will change for some, but said that accessibility has been at the “heart” of the planning process. Bus stops, it said, will be no more than about 200 metres from the pedestrianised area; it added that the street furniture was designed with input from specialist disabled groups.)
Khan’s predecessors tried, and failed, to transform Oxford Street. As mayor, Boris Johnson called pedestrianisation the “Schleswig-Holstein question of London traffic”, referring to the infamously complicated 19th-century German constitutional debate, because “everybody in abstract would love to do [it]” until they look at the “actual economic impact”. But by 2016, the tipping point had been reached – all the major mayoral candidates that year proposed pedestrianising it in principle, and when Khan won, he pledged that it would be completed by 2020. For a brief period, City Hall, Transport for London (TfL) and Westminster council appeared to be pulling in the same direction. Polling in 2018 and 2024 has shown about two-thirds of Londoners support the idea.
But the political fight over Oxford Street has often been less about how it is transformed than who gets to decide. In 2018, local opposition to Khan’s pedestrianisation plan crystallised into the creation of Capo, the Campaign Against Pedestrianisation of Oxford Street, which stood three candidates in 2018’s local elections, winning more than 1,000 votes between them. Spooked by this, Nickie Aiken, the council’s Conservative leader, used the backlash to nix the plan. Khan was furious, calling Westminster’s withdrawal “a betrayal” and claiming that £8m of public money had been wasted by the scheme’s collapse.
A decade and a pandemic later, it is finally happening because the planning authority is now held by the OSDC, which was established by the mayor’s office. The Better Oxford Street campaign, a coalition of local opponents to pedestrianisation, called this transfer of power a display of “jaw-dropping audacity” by the mayor, with the OSDC superseding the council “and its democratically elected representatives”.
As Jan Gehl observed to me, compared with some city halls around the world, London mayors have limited power. They can’t raise taxes (or introduce rent caps, legislate or control health services), which makes urban change that much harder to achieve. One thing that is under the mayor’s remit though is TfL: after he got the latter to agree to reroute their buses around the street, and with the OSDC up and running, Khan was finally in the driving seat.
What happens next week is just the beginning. The first half of Oxford Street will close to traffic on Monday – but the pedestrianisation process that follows will stretch on for well over a year.
The people behind the project are anxious that the initial testing phase is not misunderstood as a permanent project that has been built cheaply, or half heartedly. The testing process will involve a lot of people standing around with clipboards and measuring things, observing the different ways and places that pedestrians dwell. Even the picnic benches they are installing will be engaging in data collection, thanks to a “beacon”, a sensor recessed into the seat, that will measure how many people sit down, for how long, and the ambient temperature at the time.
There are other problems to navigate. On my first “site visit” to Oxford Street with East’s Archie Bashford, he showed me an example of how not to do public-realm architecture. We were on a little side street behind Oxford Circus station. There stood three vast steel plant pots, each hosting a leafless, skeletal young tree. The soil base was crisscrossed with a lattice of slats, the gaps completely stuffed with cigarette butts. The planters had become giant ash trays, which presumably hadn’t done much for the dying trees. At the root of this miserable scene were security concerns, Bashford explained – the designers had wanted to keep the soil out of reach. I was confused. “Some planters,” Lewis later explained, “are quite conducive to hiding things.” Such as knives.
This might sound like Metropolitan police hyperbole. But the knife threat is not just a scare story: weapons hidden by organised crime groups are often found in “soft landscape”, usually soil, for easy extraction and future use, removing the danger of being caught in possession.
There is a delicate balance to be struck between public safety and a more sociable public realm. The social optimist’s view is that you minimise crime in the public realm not by making it so miserable that nobody wants to visit in the first place, but by overwhelming the minority of people behaving badly with people who are behaving well. The architects at East hope that some forms of crime, such as drug dealing, will become harder, for the simple reason that it will be more visible. “Sometimes you do have to mitigate [criminal activity],” Lewis said, “but I think it’s more successful in the long term to provide an infrastructure that supports social activity, and invites it.”
Another concern is that the new Oxford Street becomes something rather more mundane: a successfully pedestrianised but ultimately disappointing place. An open-air shopping mall, a tourist trap, a hyperbranded open-air events venue, or an empty corridor after closing time. Some observers worry it could acquire some of the same problems that Barcelona’s La Rambla is still tackling. In recent decades the Catalan boulevard has been a tawdry sacrifice to tourists, largely abandoned by local residents. In an effort to avoid that outcome, there has been a great deal of communication between Barcelona and London. What would success look like in two years’ time, I asked Khan, as we lingered outside Selfridges, occasionally apologising as we sidestepped passersby. “Of course there’s an economic side,” he said. “We want to see retail doing well, we want to see the return of flagship stores. We want to see more people spending time and coming back to Oxford Street: not just first-time visitors, but return visitors.” It should also form the first stage of a wider transformation of London’s entire West End, he added. “We want to see Marylebone benefit from this, we want to see Soho benefit from this. We want to show people that this is how the heart of a global city should feel, should look, should be experienced. That will be success.”

People don’t tend to look up on Oxford Street, I’ve noticed, because they can’t – they’d be mown down.
But it turns out, if you gaze above shop-window height, that Oxford Street has a rich architectural history, stretching across styles and centuries, from the modernist Barbara Hepworth statue on the side of John Lewis to the imposing 18th-century Pantheon that hosts Marks & Spencer. It is worth your time to linger, even beyond the fundamental human right to sit down, have a sandwich and breathe some clean air.

In February, the mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, announced that Britain’s best-known thoroughfare, Oxford Street, would be pedestrianised. To the surprise of every Londoner that I have spoken to in the past few months, it is actually happening. On Monday 26 October, the busiest shopping street in Europe – or, precisely, half of its 1.2-mile stretch – will be closed to traffic, putting an end to several decades of bitter arguments, obstructions and delays. Cars, lorries, vans, taxis, buses, bicycles, ebikes, scooters will be banned. Nothing but pedestrians (and emergency vehicles) will be allowed in.
This change will mark the most remarkable transformation to the streetscape of central London since at least 2003, when Trafalgar Square was turned from a glorified roundabout into one of London’s most recognisable public spaces. It will also form the most visible part of the mayor’s legacy, whether or not Khan runs for a fourth term in 2028. Three years ago, Khan published a memoir and manifesto, Breathe, attributing his asthma to growing up inhaling London’s polluted air. For the mayor, pedestrianising Oxford Street is the culmination of a mission to create a greener city that is oriented around public health, walking and cycling.
Pedestrianisation is one thing; making Oxford Street somewhere anyone actually wants to spend time is another. For weary Londoners and anxious visitors alike, it is a headache in the form of a high street. Its primary associations are crowds, stress, dirt, noise, the tackiest incarnations of consumer capitalism, and crime. At one point during my research I approached a harried police officer in the throng outside Tottenham Court Road tube station and asked if she thought pedestrianisation would be good for Oxford Street, or make her job harder. Both, she said.
This is not to say Oxford Street is an empty, dying high street. At the last count, it receives more than 500,000 visitors every day – equivalent to the population of Edinburgh. It seems reasonable to assume that most of London’s 22 million annual foreign visitors set foot on it at some point. The street generates 5% of the capital’s economic output, and lives in the national imagination the way few others do. “When I was 17, London meant Oxford Street,” sang Everything But the Girl, in their 1988 song of the same name: “It was a little world.” And yet, nobody loves Oxford Street. During the course of writing this article, I haven’t met anyone who will even admit to liking it.
On a Sunday evening in September, I did something I had always carefully avoided doing before and cycled its full length. Even at the end of the weekend, it was overwhelming – with teenagers careening on rented ebikes and gaudy pedicabs parked in the middle of the pavement, blaring music. The pavements were thick with people, in part because the road was still thick with traffic. On another occasion, I watched a late-middle-aged woman perch awkwardly outside Ikea on a narrow black electricity box, in the absence of anywhere else to rest. For most Londoners, Oxford Street is a necessary evil, to be visited with surgical precision before fleeing the scene: a site of crime, grime and perhaps some Christmas shopping. “Who,” wondered the FT’s architecture critic in 2020, “lingers any longer than they have to in London’s worst thoroughfare?”
The grime itself is no joke. In the 1990s, when Oxford Street was known for its huge record shops such as HMV and Virgin Megastore, I remember returning to my south London home on the tube, blowing my nose and seeing a tissue full of jet-black snot. Its narrow streetway and tall buildings on either side create an “urban canyon”, trapping the heavy diesel fumes emanating from its buses and taxis (private car access has been restricted since 1972). In 2014, it was found to have the highest concentration of nitrogen dioxide pollution in the world. In the same year, the crime had become so bad that the United Arab Emirates warned its citizens to avoid the area for their own safety.
Since then it has become better known for its lawbreaking small businesses, where substantial raids have hauled in counterfeit goods and illegal vapes. This decade has seen the rise of mysterious US candy stores and empty souvenir shops that allegedly thrive thanks to tax evasion. Covid and internet shopping hit Oxford Street hard: vacancy levels soared from 4.5% in 2019 to 16.9% by early 2023, and it was often these businesses that filled the gaps. The current Google Street View images of its shopfronts, taken just two years ago, already look like a postcard from the past.
That Oxford Street has been struggling hurts the reputation of London as a whole. This is in tabloid parlance, “the nation’s high street”, home to the flagship branches of iconic department stores alongside global retail brands. Khan’s gamble is that the pedestrianisation can reverse what he conceded in 2024 was a case of “managed decline”, and will flood the street with life again.
In the offices of East, near London Fields, Julian Lewis and Archie Bashford were seated around a 4ft-long cardboard model of Oxford Street and talking animatedly about bollards. Lewis and his team are public realm architects, devoted not to buildings, but the world beyond them: signage, benches, perches, kerbs, paving, lighting, planters, trees and public art. East have carried out nearly 30 high street redesign projects in as many years, but this is the big one.
The first thing Lewis’s team did after being awarded the contract last year was to dive into the archives. The starting point was a little-known 1932 article in Good Housekeeping by Virginia Woolf. For Woolf, Oxford Street appeared as a “great rolling ribbon … the pebbly bed of a river … washed by a bright stream”. She saw it as gaudy, but also sparkling, thrilling and overwhelming, defined by the restless movement of its messy public. (Her essay also shows us how weird the street has long been – in 1932, it was apparently full of hawkers selling live tortoises.) It was these riverine characteristics that became the starting point for the thousands of material, small-scale design decisions that East are making. The “play of light on surfaces, the subtle reflectivity of a bench or a column” can all help bring out those tendencies, Bashford told me.
The pedestrianisation happening next week will cover 0.6 miles, stretching westwards from close to the Oxford Circus crossing to Selfridges. (Sadiq Khan has expressed his commitment to eventually pedestrianise all 1.2 miles of the street.) The most noticeable transformation will be how much greener it is becoming. The architects’ plan is to experiment with introducing young trees in pots, alongside new places to sit. They will use the test phase – which will last from next week until spring 2027 – to learn about how people respond to the trees. Will they become meeting points? Rest stops? Landmarks for wayfinding? Ideally they will provide respite, Lewis said, “a refuge from the flow of people, which is the river analogy again – maybe that’s optimistic, but instilling some relative calm”.
The pedestrianised zone’s edges will be marked by bollards. Lewis has strong opinions on this subject, and speaks about bollards as if they were people. “Bollards are generally horrible things,” he told me. Too often they seem “apologetic”, he said. “A misaligned, plasticky reflective strip [on a bollard] sends the message: ‘Sorry, I didn’t really mean to be here, but I need to let you know there are some vehicles nearby.’ Instead, they should be saying: ‘I’m happy to be here, because I’m doing a job.’”
An abundance of considerations go into designing the right kind of bollard, including security, maintenance, aesthetics, accessibility, climate, foot traffic, crowd flow and civic pride. Oxford Street’s bollards have to be exactly 1.2 metres apart, for reasons of HVM – hostile vehicle mitigation – but they also need to be helpful and use “the existing language of the street”. They will be made of ductile iron, because it is more resilient than cast iron: it’s springy, and doesn’t crack when you hit it. They are also matt, because shiny bollards are too flashy, and detract from the ambience. “They’re very sophisticated,” Lewis said, and he meant it.

Oxford Street does not have a place yet, it’s a non-spatial space, which is unbelievable given how famous it is.”
This is where landscape architecture and design comes in. Bus stops, it said, will be no more than about 200 metres from the pedestrianised area; it added that the street furniture was designed with input from specialist disabled groups.)
Khan’s predecessors tried, and failed, to transform Oxford Street. As mayor, Boris Johnson called pedestrianisation the “Schleswig-Holstein question of London traffic”, referring to the infamously complicated 19th-century German constitutional debate, because “everybody in abstract would love to do [it]” until they look at the “actual economic impact”. But by 2016, the tipping point had been reached – all the major mayoral candidates that year proposed pedestrianising it in principle, and when Khan won, he pledged that it would be completed by 2020. For a brief period, City Hall, Transport for London (TfL) and Westminster council appeared to be pulling in the same direction. Polling in 2018 and 2024 has shown about two-thirds of Londoners support the idea.
But the political fight over Oxford Street has often been less about how it is transformed than who gets to decide. In 2018, local opposition to Khan’s pedestrianisation plan crystallised into the creation of Capo, the Campaign Against Pedestrianisation of Oxford Street, which stood three candidates in 2018’s local elections, winning more than 1,000 votes between them. Spooked by this, Nickie Aiken, the council’s Conservative leader, used the backlash to nix the plan. Khan was furious, calling Westminster’s withdrawal “a betrayal” and claiming that £8m of public money had been wasted by the scheme’s collapse.
A decade and a pandemic later, it is finally happening because the planning authority is now held by the OSDC, which was established by the mayor’s office. The Better Oxford Street campaign, a coalition of local opponents to pedestrianisation, called this transfer of power a display of “jaw-dropping audacity” by the mayor, with the OSDC superseding the council “and its democratically elected representatives”.
As Jan Gehl observed to me, compared with some city halls around the world, London mayors have limited power. They can’t raise taxes (or introduce rent caps, legislate or control health services), which makes urban change that much harder to achieve. One thing that is under the mayor’s remit though is TfL: after he got the latter to agree to reroute their buses around the street, and with the OSDC up and running, Khan was finally in the driving seat.
What happens next week is just the beginning. The first half of Oxford Street will close to traffic on Monday – but the pedestrianisation process that follows will stretch on for well over a year.
The people behind the project are anxious that the initial testing phase is not misunderstood as a permanent project that has been built cheaply, or half heartedly. The testing process will involve a lot of people standing around with clipboards and measuring things, observing the different ways and places that pedestrians dwell. Even the picnic benches they are installing will be engaging in data collection, thanks to a “beacon”, a sensor recessed into the seat, that will measure how many people sit down, for how long, and the ambient temperature at the time.
There are other problems to navigate. On my first “site visit” to Oxford Street with East’s Archie Bashford, he showed me an example of how not to do public-realm architecture. We were on a little side street behind Oxford Circus station. There stood three vast steel plant pots, each hosting a leafless, skeletal young tree. The soil base was crisscrossed with a lattice of slats, the gaps completely stuffed with cigarette butts. The planters had become giant ash trays, which presumably hadn’t done much for the dying trees. At the root of this miserable scene were security concerns, Bashford explained – the designers had wanted to keep the soil out of reach. I was confused. “Some planters,” Lewis later explained, “are quite conducive to hiding things.” Such as knives.
This might sound like Metropolitan police hyperbole. But the knife threat is not just a scare story: weapons hidden by organised crime groups are often found in “soft landscape”, usually soil, for easy extraction and future use, removing the danger of being caught in possession.
There is a delicate balance to be struck between public safety and a more sociable public realm. The social optimist’s view is that you minimise crime in the public realm not by making it so miserable that nobody wants to visit in the first place, but by overwhelming the minority of people behaving badly with people who are behaving well. The architects at East hope that some forms of crime, such as drug dealing, will become harder, for the simple reason that it will be more visible. “Sometimes you do have to mitigate [criminal activity],” Lewis said, “but I think it’s more successful in the long term to provide an infrastructure that supports social activity, and invites it.”
Another concern is that the new Oxford Street becomes something rather more mundane: a successfully pedestrianised but ultimately disappointing place. An open-air shopping mall, a tourist trap, a hyperbranded open-air events venue, or an empty corridor after closing time. Some observers worry it could acquire some of the same problems that Barcelona’s La Rambla is still tackling. In recent decades the Catalan boulevard has been a tawdry sacrifice to tourists, largely abandoned by local residents. In an effort to avoid that outcome, there has been a great deal of communication between Barcelona and London. Barcelona’s city hall is keenly watching Oxford Street, Nabeel Khan told me, and East’s architects have visited Barcelona to procure their data-gathering seating.
What would success look like in two years’ time, I asked Khan, as we lingered outside Selfridges, occasionally apologising as we sidestepped passersby. “Of course there’s an economic side,” he said. “We want to see retail doing well, we want to see the return of flagship stores. We want to see more people spending time and coming back to Oxford Street: not just first-time visitors, but return visitors.” It should also form the first stage of a wider transformation of London’s entire West End, he added. “We want to see Marylebone benefit from this, we want to see Soho benefit from this. We want to show people that this is how the heart of a global city should feel, should look, should be experienced. That will be success.”
Archie Bashford believes the change in atmosphere will be profound: “Even if we were doing nothing else, and they just shut the street, it would feel amazing and transgressive.” In just a few weeks’ time, visitors will be able to look up at Oxford Street’s glittering Christmas lights without worrying about being run over. People don’t tend to look up on Oxford Street, I’ve noticed, because they can’t – they’d be mown down.
But it turns out, if you gaze above shop-window height, that Oxford Street has a rich architectural history, stretching across styles and centuries, from the modernist Barbara Hepworth statue on the side of John Lewis to the imposing 18th-century Pantheon that hosts Marks & Spencer. It is worth your time to linger, even beyond the fundamental human right to sit down, have a sandwich and breathe some clean air.

title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion in Cambridge Analytica case
content_c:
Meta ordered to pay $25 billion in Cambridge Analytica case
October 21, 2026
US tech giant Meta, owner of Facebook, was ordered to pay $25 billion (around €22.5 billion) to the US state of New Mexico after a jury found Facebook deceived its users over privacy and content moderation.
"Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data. This was false," Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order following the Wednesday verdict.
The case links back to the 2016 Cambridge Analytica scandal, when a third-party quiz harvested the data of some 87 million Facebook profiles and sold it to the UK-based political consulting firm. The firm used the data for targeted ads, including campaign ads for Donald Trump's first presidential run.
New Mexico rejects deal with Meta
Nearly all US states agreed to settle with Facebook over a myriad of legal issues for an overall payment of $18 billion in August. This included releasing the company from future liability for the Cambridge Analytica breach.
New Mexico refused to settle and filed a lawsuit against the platform. Prosecutors claimed that the social network deceived the state's entire population of some 2.1 million people by its public statements on privacy. The US state also argued that Facebook allowed the spread of misinformation and violent content.
In turn, the company's lawyers said the state failed to prove people were actually harmed by Facebook's statements, and claimed the platform had robust content moderation.
In September, a jury found Facebook liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws. Meta pledged to "continue to defend ourselves against efforts to distort our record."
Meta's billions could go to New Mexico's education system
Following the jury's decision last month, it was up to the court to determine how much Meta would pay the state. While the $25 billion fine is lower than the $35 billion to $40 billion demanded by the New Mexico prosecutors, it far exceeds the cap of $3.45 billion suggested by Meta's lawyers.
"This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is money, and the value of its stock price," New Mexico attorney Randi McGinn said during the trial.
On Wednesday, New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez said the outcome should be "an unambiguous message" to Silicon Valley.
While noting that the money will likely be tied up due to appeals, Torrez also noted that the fine is legally due to be paid into New Mexico's education fund.
"We may have paid for the construction of schools for the next 100 years," he said.
The case is the latest in the string of legal challenges large social media companies face in the US and other parts of the world, including the separate August verdict in New Mexico ordering Facebook to pay $567 million over harm to children.
Edited by: Sean Sinico

title: Osteuropa-Experte über Ukraine-Gespräche: "Keine großen Hoffnungen"
content_c:
Osteuropa-Experte über Ukraine-Gespräche "Keine großen Hoffnungen"
Russland hat sich bereit gezeigt, die Gespräche mit den USA und der Ukraine wieder aufzunehmen. Aber sind Fortschritte wahrscheinlich? Osteuropa-Experte Umland zeigt sich im tagesschau24-Interview skeptisch.
tagesschau24: Es gibt die Meldung, der Kreml sei bereit, ab Mitte November wieder zu verhandeln - mit den USA und der Ukraine. Was ist davon zu halten?
Andreas Umland: Zurzeit nicht viel, denn dieses Verhandlungstheater gibt es ja schon viele Jahre, im Grunde schon seit 2014. Und da geht es immer darum, was Russland im Austausch für einen Waffenstillstand und für Frieden bekommen kann. Also wie viel ukrainisches Territorium abgegeben wird, wie viel ukrainische Souveränität abgegeben wird. Insofern habe ich da bisher keine großen Hoffnungen.
Was ich mir allerdings vorstellen könnte, ist, dass vielleicht der innere Druck in Russland durch die ukrainische Langstreckenangriffe steigt, und dass es dann vielleicht tatsächlich eine Fraktion in Moskau geben wird, die sich in Richtung eines Waffenstillstands orientieren wird. Vielleicht wird sich das ändern, wenn sich die ökonomischen Probleme, die Russland derzeit schon hat, verstärken.
Dann machen solche Verhandlungen einen Sinn. Aber zurzeit kann man da nur mit weiterem Verhandlungstheater rechnen.
"Der Eroberer will immer Frieden. So ist das bei Putin auch"
tagesschau24: Außerdem sagte der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj bei Fox News, man sei bereit, die Frontlinie einzufrieren. Ist das etwas, was den Kreml ködern könnte?
Umland: Ich fürchte nicht. Denn diese Position der Ukraine gibt es schon seit circa anderthalb Jahren. Das hat Selenskyj schon im Frühjahr 2025 explizit vorgeschlagen und seitdem mehrere Male. Er hat auch teilweise Waffenstillstände vorgeschlagen, zum Beispiel ein Einstellen der Langstreckenangriffe auf die Energieinfrastruktur oder eine Art Waffenstillstand im Schwarzen Meer.
All diese Vorschläge hat Russland abgelehnt, denn Russland möchte im Gegenzug für einen Waffenstillstand Gebiet haben. So ist das ja immer. Schon der Militärtheoretiker Carl von Clausewitz sagte vor knapp 200 Jahren: Der Eroberer will keinen Krieg, der Eroberer will nur friedlich in das Nachbarland einmarschieren und die Gebiete übernehmen. Der Eroberer will immer Frieden. Und so ist das bei Putin jetzt auch.
"Konferenz der Großmächte - das ist die große Furcht"
tagesschau24: Droht die Ukraine momentan zwischen den USA und Russland zermahlen zu werden - zumal der Wind aus den USA eher wieder pro Russland weht?
Umland: Ja, die Befürchtung ist, dass man auf ein zweites Jalta zusteuert, also eine Konferenz der Großmächte, von denen Osteuropa aufgeteilt wird, und wo die osteuropäischen Nationen überhaupt nichts mehr beizutragen haben.
Das ist die große Furcht. Und es ist auch, glaube ich, Putins Ziel, wieder zu dem Jalta-System zurückzukommen: Dass die Großmächte alleine besprechen, was mit den kleineren Staaten zu machen ist.
"Russische Unterstützung des Wahlkampfs der Republikaner"
tagesschau24: Was müssen wir von diesem Verhältnis zwischen den USA und Russland erwarten? Heute gab es die Meldung, dass der in Russland inhaftierte US-amerikanische Lehrer Stephen Hubbard freigelassen wurde. Gleichzeitig hieß es aus Russland, man habe den ersten Diesel Richtung USA verschifft. Ist das eine Annäherung, bei der die Ukraine und vielleicht Europa komplett auf der Strecke bleiben?
Umland: Letztlich ist das nicht so bedeutsam. Es geht hier in erster Linie um den amerikanischen Wahlkampf. Putin versucht nun, Trump mit solchen positiven Signalen zu unterstützen. Der eigentliche Skandal ist ja bei Hubbard, der im Moment seiner Inhaftierung in der Ostukraine 72 Jahre alt war, dass er überhaupt so lange im russischen Gefängnis gesessen hat.
Bei den Diesellieferungen möchte Russland das Sanktionsregime aufbrechen. Aber die vereinbarten Liefermengen sind so gering, dass sie eigentlich gar keine Auswirkung haben werden auf den Dieselpreis in den USA. Man schafft zwar positive Signale, aber ich glaube nicht, dass sich materiell irgendetwas ändern wird. Das ist im Grunde eine Art russische Unterstützung des Wahlkampfs der Republikaner.
Hat Europa genug "Eigeninteresse", die Ukraine zu unterstützen?
tagesschau24: Was können wir Europäer noch ausrichten? In Europa stehen viele Regierungen unter Druck, in manchen Ländern stehen bald Wahlen an. Auch die Bundesregierung steht enorm unter Druck. Wie stark ist Europa noch, dass wir überhaupt mitreden können?
Umland: Die Summe der europäischen Staaten ist ja mächtig. Und es gibt nicht nur europäische Staaten, die die Ukraine unterstützen, sondern zum Beispiel auch Japan, Australien oder Kanada. Die Koalition ist auch ohne die USA groß.
Die Frage ist, inwieweit die europäischen Länder ein Eigeninteresse zumindest an einem ukrainischen Teilsieg entwickeln - also daran, dass die Ukraine nicht weiteres Gebiet verliert - und daran, einen Waffenstillstand entlang der heutigen Frontlinie durchzusetzen.
Das Eigeninteresse könnte zum Beispiel darin bestehen, dass man weitere Flüchtlinge aus der Ukraine verhindern will, womöglich Millionen von Flüchtlingen. Oder dass man verhindern will, dass wenn Russland aus diesem Krieg mit einer Art Teilsieg herauskommt, mit einer Teilkapitulation der Ukraine, dass Russland dann seine Armee in andere europäische Staaten schickt, wie zum Beispiel in die baltischen Staaten, die Mitglieder der NATO und der Europäischen Union sind. Dann wären wir laut NATO-Vertrag und EU-Vertrag verpflichtet, an einem Krieg gegen Russland teilzunehmen.
Wenn wir ein Interesse haben, die Flüchtlinge und die Ausweitung des Krieges in einen Krieg gegen NATO und EU zu verhindern, dann müsste es eigentlich genug Eigeninteresse der europäischen Staaten geben, die Ukraine zumindest beim Aufrechterhalten der jetzigen Frontlinie zu unterstützen.
Was würde ein Sieg der Demokraten bei den Midterms bedeuten?
tagesschau24: In zwei Wochen sind die US-Zwischenwahlen, und alles deutet auf eine Niederlage für die Republikaner hin. Mindestens eine der Kammern im Kongress wird wohl an die Demokraten gehen. Was ändert sich da für Europa, was für die Ukraine und was für die Konstellation, über die wir eben gesprochen haben?
Umland: Das ist für mich schwer einzuschätzen, weil sich dann natürlich sehr viele Dinge in der Innenpolitik ändern würden. Aber tendenziell sind die Demokraten pro-ukrainischer als die Republikaner und natürlich sehr viel pro-ukrainischer als die jetzige US-Administration.
Das Weiße Haus vertritt jetzt in vieler Hinsicht eine pro-russische Position, bei den Abstimmungen in der UNO etwa stimmen Russland und die USA neuerdings oft gemeinsam ab. Und eben dieses Weiße Haus hat unter Trump auch die materielle Unterstützung der Ukraine vollständig eingestellt.
Insofern hoffe ich, dass sich dann mit einem Machtwechsel zumindest im Repräsentantenhaus und vielleicht auch im Senat die Gesamtpolitik der USA gegenüber der Ukraine verbessert. Allerdings wird es wahrscheinlich auch viele innenpolitische Auswirkungen geben, die womöglich die Aufmerksamkeit der Amerikaner für das Weltgeschehen reduzieren wird. Und das wäre dann wieder negativ für die Ukraine.
Das Gespräch führte Bernd Rasem, tagesschau24. Für die schriftliche Fassung wurde das Interview angepasst.
